articles.title_orig: McDonald's bets on hand-breaded chicken, AI drive-throughs to fend off Burger King
articles.title_zh: McDonald's bets on hand-breaded chicken, AI drive-throughs to fend off Burger King
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO, IL — McDonald's (MCD) is making a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of 90s-style restaurants to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King.
At its investor day in Chicago, the fast food giant unveiled a new set of ambitious goals and investments as part of its growth plan, following a rocky second quarter that resulted in 0.8% US same-store sales growth versus Burger King's whopping 8.5% growth.
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 to support restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
Franchisees are encouraged to adopt the plan in phases. One franchisee operator told Yahoo Finance they are skating on thin margins with higher ingredient, labor, and rent costs, making another costly redesign difficult, especially in a high-interest-rate environment.
Deploying the entire NEXT strategy will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per restaurant. Operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a remodel cycle every 10 years, per McDonald's.
"You start with the opportunity, which we think is really clear and compelling," McDonald's CFO Ian Borden told Yahoo Finance. "We think it's going to provide a really strong return for our operators and for McDonald's."
It remains to be seen whether the strategic growth plan can turn around McDonald's stock. McDonald's shares have struggled to entice investors to take a bite this year, declining 18% year to date, compared to a 4.6% gain for Burger King's parent company stock, Restaurant Brands International (QSR), and 13% gain for the S&P 500 (^GSPC).
McDonald's stock fell 5% on Wednesday.
Chicken, but 'Make it Golden'
Part of the strategy is a commitment called "Make it Golden," which doubles down on food, hospitality, and employee training.
After Burger King overhauled its chicken nugget recipe, McDonald's is doing something similar by piloting hand-breaded chicken.
The chicken comes frozen, marinated, dipped in batter, and hand-breaded, Jacques Mignault, McDonald's Global Chief Restaurant Officer, told Yahoo Finance. The secret is to flip the chicken seven times.
McDonald's is targeting a 1.5% gain in market share, with the chicken and beverage categories leading the way (crafted sodas are another major focus for McDonald's). It expects to add more US restaurants to the hand-breaded chicken pilot in early 2027.
Mignault said the new chicken is "actually beating the competition from a taste and quality standpoint" in Asian markets. He added that the company has also started testing bone-in wings.

articles.title_orig: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.title_zh: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.content_orig:
• Iran president speaks: In his UN General Assembly address, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will never bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• Trump on Iran: The US president said yesterday that he faces a decision between annihilating Iran or making a deal to end the war. The US said delegations from both countries held talks on the sidelines through mediators.
• Zelensky gives remarks later: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said he was ready for trilateral talks with Russia and US to end the war in Ukraine, is also speaking today.
• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on Venezuela to enact reforms.
Why the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical sticking point in the Iran war
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian brought up the Strait of Hormuz earlier in his speech to the UN General Assembly. Months after the US and Israel launched the war with Iran, the strait remains at the center of the conflict and the global energy crisis.
Talks between Persian Gulf diplomats and Iranian officials — which were set to discuss an Omani plan for reopening the waterway to tanker traffic — were postponed indefinitely earlier this month.
Why it’s so significant: There are few places more strategically important to the global economy than the waterway, located between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Before the war, around 20% of global oil production flowed through the strait.
The waterway is only about 24 miles across at its narrowest point. Bolstered by sea mines, missiles and miles of coastline, Iran has long had the upper hand for controlling the shipping lane.
The US initially underestimated Iran’s willingness to close the strait — a strategic error that Tehran has capitalized on by leveraging its ability to threaten commercial shipping and prolong the war.
The current state-of-play: Despite shipping traffic remaining depressed, US President Donald Trump has insisted the state of the waterway is acceptable for now. In recent weeks, more tankers have moved through the strait due to the US military clearing mines and escorting vessels through the passage.
But commercial ships still face the threat of Iranian attacks, and there are questions around how long the US military can credibly maintain its substantial commitment of ships and resources to the strait.
What happens next: Trump administration officials have privately indicated they want to refocus negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and not reopening the strait, according to three sources familiar with the matter.
Iranian officials have signaled that they would be open to nuclear negotiations with the US — but only when the strait issue is resolved and the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, a regional source told CNN.
As a result, getting the ball rolling on a framework to reopen the waterway is likely a critical step to pave the way for talks on an overall end to the war.
CNN’s John Liu, Chris Isidore, Nadeen Ebrahim, Kylie Atwood, Zachary Cohen, Lauren Kent, Annette Choi and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.
Ahead of Zelensky's remarks at UNGA, catch up on the status of the war in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will speak at the UN General Assembly later today.
Get up to speed on what’s been happening on the ground as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds past four and a half years, with no sign of stopping anytime soon:
- No letup with strikes: Russia continues to hit Kyiv and other cities throughout Ukraine with drones and missiles, as Ukraine has been hammering Russian fuel infrastructure for months. Today, Russia targeted warehouses in Odesa, areas of Kyiv and a Zaporizhzhia shopping center. Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out its largest-ever drone attack on the Russian capital and surrounding area as voting in parliamentary elections entered the final day. Earlier this month, a Russian drone hit a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland as a group of former Western officials traveled out of the country, and NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank remain on high alert.
- Trump claims agreement: US President Donald Trump last Tuesday said Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets amid concerns over the global spike in fuel prices — but both Zelensky and the Kremlin later described it as a proposal rather than a firm agreement.
- Russian missile attacks: Russia has increasingly been launching high-speed missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defense interceptors. That shortage has been compounded by a global supply crunch due to the Iran war.
- Ukraine targets logistics hubs: Ukraine, meanwhile, has recently struck deep into Russian territory, sparking fuel shortages. Kyiv has also stepped up attacks on Ozon logistics hubs in Russia — a competitor to the frequently targeted e-commerce giant Wildberries — as it seeks to undermine Moscow’s war-driven economy.
- First visit from US envoys: Special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner pushed for a return to trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in a meeting with top Ukrainian officials earlier this month, which marked their first trip to Kyiv since the war began. The talks followed intensive meetings between the US team and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Russia hit Kyiv a day after the visit.
CNN’s Laura Sharman, Svitlana Vlasova, Darya Tarasova, Ivana Kottasová, Sophie Tanno, Lex Harvey, Chris Isidore, Matt Egan, Nathan Hodge, Clare Sebastian, Zahra Ullah, Anna Chernova, Katharina Krebs, Kosta Gak, Sophie Tanno, Billy Stockwell and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.
Rubio: 'No discussion' of extending US final withdrawal from Iraq
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been “no discussion” of extending the US’ final withdrawal from Iraq, which is slated for the end of this month.
The US military presence in Iraq is scheduled to officially end on September 30 after more than two decades, following a 2024 agreement to withdraw remaining troops after the end of the ISIS campaign.
Still, Baghdad has struggled to deal with the militias within its country. Iranian-backed militia in Iraq have launched waves of strikes on US and allied interests amid the war in Iran.
Rubio, who met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the UN General Assembly on Monday, said al-Zaidi did not ask the US to extend its presence.
President Donald Trump also saw al-Zaidi “briefly” on Tuesday night, Rubio told reporters in New York.
Responding to a question from CNN, Rubio said the US has “zero doubt” of al-Zaidi’s commitment to try to control the Iraqi militias but noted that it is “a massive challenge.”
The top US diplomat said the Iraqi prime minister has “achieved certain things” with regard to the militias, noting that “at least three militias have disarmed and have basically joined the national government.”
“As we’ve told him, we want him to succeed. We think he gives the world and Iraq the best chance to succeed. I think he has the right intentions. I think he has the right motivations. He’s very intelligent and a very willing partner in this regard, and we’re going to do everything we can to help him achieve the results,” he said.
“Nothing would be more important for Iraq than to deal with this and to bring all the arms in that country under the control of the national government,” Rubio added.

NFL Network reports that Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart “is expected to have knee surgery that will lead to a full recovery but end his 2026 season.”

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial.
Weinstein, who pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree criminal sexual act, appeared in the downtown Manhattan courtroom in a wheelchair, his hands cuffed to his seat.
In a victim impact statement read aloud in the courtroom, Haley said Weinstein “abused his position and power,” causing a “devastating effect on my life and security.”
“It is a life sentence for me,” Haley said.
Weinstein also addressed the court, again denying the allegations against him while apologizing to “anyone I may have hurt by my actions.”
“I am not a perfect person,” he said, “but I am a person who has made mistakes.” He later added: “I am not a violent man.”
Judge Curtis Farber excoriated Weinstein before handing down his sentence. “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility,” the judge told the former entertainment industry kingmaker.
Farber said Weinstein’s 15-year sentence will be followed by five years of supervised release and a requirement that he register as a sex offender.
Wednesday’s sentencing came after a protracted series of trials, appeals and courtroom proceedings that have kept Weinstein behind bars since his arrest in 2018, one of the key events of the #MeToo movement.
Weinstein was originally convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving former aspiring actor Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley. He was sentenced to 23 years in prison. But his conviction was overturned in 2024 by a New York state appeals court, and a judge ordered a new trial.
Weinstein was again found guilty in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, who testified that he forcibly performed oral sex on her in his New York City apartment in 2006. The same jury acquitted him of a separate criminal sex act charge involving allegations from former model Kaja Sokola.
The jurors at Weinstein’s second New York trial could not reach a verdict on the charge related to Mann’s allegation, and a third trial on that charge also ended in a hung jury. In late June, prosecutors declined to try the Mann case a fourth time.
Weinstein was separately convicted in Los Angeles in December 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault related to a 2013 assault of an Italian actor and model. He was sentenced by a Los Angeles judge to 16 years in prison in February 2023.
He is set to be resentenced in L.A. after an appeals court vacated his original sentence.
The former producer and film distributor vehemently denies all allegations of sexual misconduct, insisting his sexual encounters were consensual. In all, more than 80 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault or harassment.
Weinstein once lorded over Hollywood. Miramax, his first distribution label, released seminal independent films like “Clerks” and “Pulp Fiction.” He won an Oscar as a producer of “Shakespeare in Love.” In the early 2010s, his second distribution company scored back-to-back best picture wins for “The King’s Speech” and “The Artist.”
But his reign came crashing down in 2017 after The New York Times and The New Yorker published exposés detailing his alleged pattern of sexual harassment and assault. The first wave of accusations against him in 2017 propelled the #MeToo movement, a reckoning with sexual misconduct by powerful people in high-profile professions.
In recent years, Weinstein’s health has visibly declined, and he has faced various medical issues, including diagnoses of bone marrow cancer, kidney disease and diabetes. He has been held at the Bellevue Hospital prison ward, and he will remain there until he is sent to a state prison.

articles.title_orig: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by February, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by February, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
Nearly half a million people across the world could lose their lives by February due to El Niño-driven extreme heat, according to a sobering new report.
El Niño, a natural climate pattern which typically ramps up global temperature, has now crossed into super-sized territory and is on its way to becoming record-breakingly strong.
Combined with the global warming the planet is already experiencing from fossil fuel pollution, the heat consequences could be devastating, according to the analysis from the Climate Impact Lab, a team of scientists, economists and data engineers headquartered at the University of Chicago, and published Wednesday.
🌡️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app.
Heat is the most deadly form of extreme weather — although heat deaths are not well-tracked, even in rich nations. The report estimates the heat from El Niño could take 451,000 lives between June 2026, when it arrived, and February 2027. Those deaths would be in addition to the usual number of heat-related deaths.
The researchers believe this number is likely to rise — El Nino is expected to last until the Northern Hemisphere spring, meaning its heat impacts will linger into the summer months.
The deaths from extreme heat would also come in addition to those expected from other El Niño-fueled extreme weather, including fires, floods and droughts, according to the report.
The report has not yet been peer-reviewed but uses peer-reviewed methodology to reach its conclusions.
“We have long been able to predict the impacts of temperatures on crops, and now we can predict their impact on the worst outcome — death,” said Michael Greenstone, a report author, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and an economics professor at the University of Chicago.
“This is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” he added.
Scientists project that El Niño will push global land temperatures up 1.2 degrees Celsius (2.1 Fahrenheit) above normal in the coming months. This unusual warmth is exactly what climate change is projected to bring in 20 years time, and will lead to 44% more days of extreme heat than would be expected in a normal year, according to the study.
The current El Niño is a “postcard from our future” that’s arriving before the world’s had time to adapt, the authors write.
The regions expected to be most affected are overwhelmingly in the Global South. The report identifies Nigeria as where the most El Niño heat deaths are expected, with a projected 31,400 lives lost. Other countries at high risk include Indonesia, Sudan, India and Brazil. The United States is also in the top 20 affected countries, with a projected 3,500 deaths.

- The forecast is just the beginning. We’ll send you expert coverage and the stories behind the weather — so you always know more than just the number. Sign up for the newsletter
The report combined peer-reviewed methods on the relationship between temperature in more than 24,000 regions across the world and mortality and seasonal temperature forecasts. The death projections were compared to the same months of an average year between 1996 and 2025.
The study is currently awaiting peer-review, but the scientists said they released the shorter report first due to El Nino’s rapid strengthening. “Given that there is still time now for policymakers and others to take action to prevent these deaths, we felt our findings couldn’t wait for the peer review process to play out. That would certainly be too late to act for this El Niño cycle,” said a Climate Impact Lab spokesperson.
Measures countries can take include early heat warnings, health action plans, ensuring cooling and hydration centers are available and expanding healthcare coverage, the report says.
“Increasing emergency response and better targeting our efforts can save many lives this year,” said report co-author Tamma Carleton, faculty head of research for the Climate Impact Lab and an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley. “But 20 years from now, once today’s extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don’t want to be in a constant state of emergency.”

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.
The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
"It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media.
The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

articles.title_orig: Where a powerful nor’easter could hit hardest this weekend
articles.title_zh: Where a powerful nor’easter could hit hardest this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Nor'easter with coastal flooding, winds, rain will lash East Coast
Coastal flooding is already affecting the mid-Atlantic as a nor'easter targets areas from Virginia to New England.
A nor'easter will bring coastal flooding, high surf, wind and rain to parts of the East Coast through the weekend, with impacts from North Carolina and the Virginia Tidewater, to the Jersey Shore and New England.
The nor'easter hasn't yet gained strength. But the pressure difference between low pressure off the East Coast and high pressure over eastern Canada is driving gusty winds along the Eastern Seaboard.
Some gusts are topping 40 mph along the coast from Delaware to the Virginia Tidewater.
And those persistent winds are piling water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday morning's high tide.
Flooding was reported at one intersection in downtown Norfolk, Virginia, early Wednesday morning, according to local news.

Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days.
- Through Thursday: Coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds from New Jersey to northern Outer Banks of North Carolina
- Friday: Rain, possibly heavy, stronger winds, and coastal flooding arrive in parts of southeast New England, Long Island; coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds continue from New Jersey to Virginia Tidewater, northern North Carolina.
- Saturday: Locally heavy rain, strong winds possible over much of coastal, southern New England. High tide coastal flooding from New England to at least parts of the mid-Atlantic coast once again. Some at least light bands of rain possible as far west as Hudson Valley, New Jersey.
- Sunday: Nor'easter weakens, but rain showers, some gusty winds could linger over much of New England, possibly the Hudson Valley.
The map below shows the severity of coastal flooding forecast at high tide through Friday night or early Saturday, color coded by severity.
The most significant coastal flooding will be from the southern New Jersey shore to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, including the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay.
This flooding will happen for multiple high tides, possibly five or more, into at least early this weekend in these areas.
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is possible along stretches of these beaches.
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will also develop in parts of coastal New England by late Friday into the weekend.
We're expecting the heaviest rain to fall over coastal New England from Friday through the weekend.
This could lead to flash flooding, especially in urban areas, including the Boston metro.
It could also compound any coastal flooding at high tide in parts of southeast New England.
Much lighter rainfall accumulations are expected farther west, in the light green colors in the map below.
In the New York City metro, the heaviest rainfall is expected in eastern Long Island, with less rain farther west in the New Jersey suburbs.
The strongest winds with this nor'easter are expected this weekend from coastal and southeast New England to eastern Long Island, with some gusts over 50 mph possible, at times.
In these areas, some downed tree limbs and power outages are possible, including the Boston metro, Providence and Cape Cod.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible farther down the coast from the Jersey Shore to Delaware, and the Virginia Tidewater.
Here are some tips to keep in mind if you plan to travel to the Northeast into this weekend:
- Northeast major hub airports: Delays are most likely at Boston-Logan this weekend and are possible, at times, at NYC's three major airports through the weekend
- Roads: Some downed tree limbs, trees and flash flooding are possible in southeast and coastal New England, as well as eastern Long Island. Avoid coastal areas from northern North Carolina to southeast New England around any high tides into the weekend.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter?)
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

articles.title_orig: US stocks drift after oil prices halt their weeklong drop
articles.title_zh: US stocks drift after oil prices halt their weeklong drop
articles.content_orig:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on August 05, 2026 in New York City.
Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
Declines in utilities, consumer discretionary and communication services stocks led the broader market's fall, with the three sectors shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.087%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since June 2024 at 4.887%.
2-year yield vs. 10-year yield, 1-day
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 73% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, though the index is about 0.8% off from its all-time high.

McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
Selig tells CNBC activity on "mentions" contracts are concerning
Michael Selig, President Donald Trump's nominee to serve as Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairman, testifies in a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on his nomination on Capitol Hill, Nov. 19, 2025.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.
Selig also told CNBC the federal regulator has a zero tolerance policy on wash trading, after growing concerns that Kalshi has wash trading on its perpetual futures trades. The Wall Street Journal reported the CFTC is looking into the trades.
The chairman also touched on Kalshi's efforts to introduce margin trading to traders. Selig said the CFTC is evaluating the proposal and that it will allow only traders meeting "stringent eligibility criteria" to participate.
10-year Treasury yield scores fresh 19-year high
Treasury yields raced higher on Wednesday as new services and manufacturing sector data increased worry of further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday he expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further to tame inflation.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way. Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded," he said in remarks for a housing conference in Chicago.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he added. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Barr labeled last week's quarter percentage point rate hike "important action" for policy that was "out of position" in getting inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.
The remarks came as S&P Global reported that its flash readings on services and manufacturing hit their highest levels since 2021. Price pressures are also surged, posting their highest readings since October 2022.
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.
The S&P 500 lost 0.1% just after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 156 points, or 0.3%.

articles.title_orig: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.title_zh: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.content_orig:
US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that an "illegal alien" had been the subject of a targeted vehicle stop but pushed back against suggestions he had been given inadequate medical care.
The incident comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
The ICE agent who shot him - who joined the agency last year - was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources told the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
The Austin Police Department released footage from officers responding to the scene, but did not show what led to the incident.
On Tuesday, DHS pushed back against what it called "false narratives" surrounding what had happened, blaming sanctuary cities and media for "spreading lies" and discouraging people from resisting officers and evading arrest.
"Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement to the BBC.
DHS said the man, whom they did not name, was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop" and that his work permit expired last year.
"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job by removing dangerous illegal aliens from our communities and making America safe again," Mullin said.
The Austin Police Department, which was not involved in the incident, released dashcam and body camera footage on Tuesday showing its officers at the scene.
It does not show the shooting, but several gunshots can be heard in one dashcam clip, while another shows officers approaching Garces Perez's car and detaining him. At one point, Garces Perez's t-shirt is cut to reveal what appears to be a single gunshot in his back.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
In its statement on Tuesday, DHS said Garces Perez had received medical care "around the clock" and denied claims he received no pain medication and was forced to sleep on the floor.
"This alien was released from the hospital and arrived at the detention facility just a few hours later, where he slept on a bed," DHS said.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
DHS said on Tuesday that ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin".
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.title_orig: Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
articles.title_zh: Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
articles.content_orig:
Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
Growing up, I had a knack for getting distracted on school field trips to museums and art galleries.
Teachers marched us through halls of what felt like the same Baroque painting over and over. Endless soft bodies painted against pale blue skies, their stories offered up with little explanation.
It didn't feel like any of it was meant to be fun.
Then I discovered Coco, the self-described "time-traveling tart."
The brainchild and alter ego of comedian Max Norman, Coco — 6 foot 7 without heels — leads interactive and (mostly) factual tours through galleries in London and beyond.
During the Edinburgh Fringe Festival last month, she made her way to the National Galleries of Scotland for what was billed as a "cheeky romp" uncovering the "gossip, glamour and glorious absurdity hiding behind the art."
Coco had us curtsy before paintings of kings and queens of Great Britain's past, then treated us to lessons about the indulgences and insecurities that made them feel all too human.
We played dead on the floor in a lesson about the fall of the Jacobites in 18th century Scotland (let's just say swords are no match for guns).
Then we all eagerly galloped like horses from one gallery room to the next. I do not remember why — which may have been the point.
Norman created Coco as "revenge" on his artist mother, who used to drag him through art galleries across London.
For anyone who spent their own childhood staring blankly at an Old Master while waiting for someone (anyone!) to make it interesting, Coco feels less like revenge — and more like justice.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.content_orig:
No surprise here: “Patient Zero,” the song Taylor Swift announced Tuesday, is not an orphan or a one-off. The pop superstar followed news of the single a day later with her Wednesday morning reveal for a release that includes four new tracks and will also be out this Friday — “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore.”
A visit to pre-order pages shows that the new songs, besides the already announced “Patient Zero,” are “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon,” listed as tracks 13-16 on the newly expanded version of her 2025 “Showgirl” album.
On social media, Swift wrote, “About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback, my two collaborators on this album. Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs is out on Friday and available to pre-order and save now.”
Swifties had long assumed there would be no deluxe or bonus-filled edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” because, at the time, Swift had assured fans that she felt pleased with the exact 12-song configuration she was putting out and did want to augment it with anything she might have left on the cutting room floor. But, as fans now learn, that didn’t preclude coming up with additional material after the fact, which the singer is saying came out in a spontaneous explosion of post-release exhilaration with her two collaborators on that album.
Prior to “Showgirl,” she hadn’t worked with the dynamic duo of Max Martin and Shellback since 2018’s “Reputation,” but clearly the reunion took in a big way.
Eagle-eyed Swifties noted that Swift had quietly teased this project some time ago, by including the phrase “Patient for the encore” to the side of the frame in her music video for the “Showgirl” single “Opalite.”
Much more recently, she had given fans Easter eggs in puzzle form with a pre-taped sketch that aired as part of the Emmys telecast. There; Swift, in character as a “Law & Order: SVU” detective, said, “I think what we’re going to be looking for is hiding in plain sight.” She then stared into the camera and uttered several seeming nonsense phrases or words: “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south.” Fans eventually figured out that if you took the third letter from each of those utterances, they gave up the letters that form the word “encore.”
The announcement of the “Encore” edition also settles another point of trivia that had come up when Swift revealed the “Patient Zero” single was imminent on Tuesday. Many pointed out that Swift was not lately in the habit of releasing a stand-alone single ahead of an album actually coming out; the last time she had done so was with “Me!” being released months ahead of “Lover” in 2019. Now that everyone knows the “Encore” collection is coming out the same hour as the single, it’s clear she’s not breaking with that recent pattern after all.
The new release features cover photography by the team of fashion photographers Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott, continuing the imagery they created ffor the original “Showgirl” album.
No physical release has been announced for the expanded project, which hits DSPs as Thursday night turns into Friday morning. The streaming service Apple Music does show the track list as being broken down into Disc 1 (the original 12 tracks) and Disc 2 (the four newly released songs), but it’s unclear if that augurs for a two-disc vinyl or CD edition. Spotify has the 16 tracks listed in a single running order.
For now, the release of the four “Showgirl” addenda puts to bed previous widespread conjecture that Swift was certain to put out “Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)” this fall to celebrate the 20th anniversary of her debut album. But setting that aside for newly written songs is a tradeoff most fans will be happy with. So, “Our Song (Middle Aged Version)” can wait.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.content_orig:
The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats.
Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing her death on 25 August with a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.
But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.
According to Billboard, the lawsuit filed in a Tennessee court reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”
Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.
He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”
Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”
Seaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.
Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”
The chancery court in Nashville will now consider the restraining order filing. The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.
Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.
She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.

articles.title_orig: Spotify is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of 'Taste Profile'
articles.title_zh: Spotify is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of 'Taste Profile'
articles.content_orig:
Spotify is giving listeners a new tool to shape the recommendations it delivers to their app’s Home feed.
The music streaming giant on Wednesday began rolling out a feature called “Taste Profile” to its Premium subscribers in the U.S. that allows users to see, for the first time, how Spotify understands their taste across music and other audio. Users can request changes using natural language commands to fine-tune their recommendations, or make broader changes.
Powered by Spotify’s AI, Taste Profile was unveiled in March at the SXSW conference in Austin by Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström. However, the feature was initially available in beta only to listeners based in New Zealand.
Now, the feature is arriving in Spotify’s largest market in terms of traffic and revenue, where it will be put to a larger test among listeners aged 18 and up.
In some ways, Taste Profile essentially gives you the keys to Spotify’s algorithm. It is how the streaming platform chooses what music and podcasts to suggest, including in its flagship Discover Weekly playlist, its Made for You recommendations, and the highly anticipated annual review known as Spotify Wrapped.
Though Spotify’s algorithmic understanding of a listener’s habits is largely credited as the secret to its success, those recommendations don’t always reflect users’ evolving tastes. The platform often ends up recommending too-similar music when a user would rather branch out.
Now, by editing their Taste Profile directly, Spotify users can request more variety or ask for more or less of a certain genre, artist, or overall vibe.
The feature could be used to remove recommendations based on music that users may regularly stream, but not necessarily care to see more of — for instance, sleep sounds played at night, or whatever music a teenager plays while in the car on their parent’s account.
Until now, Spotify has offered some options to remove music from your Taste Profile, but they only let you exclude certain tracks or playlists. More recently, the company added a much-requested toggle switch that would prevent kids’ music from impacting their parents’ recommendations.
To access Taste Profiles on the mobile app, first tap on your profile pic, then scroll down and select Taste Profile. From here, you’ll be able to explore how Spotify currently understands your taste across music, podcasts, and audiobooks. Under “Tell us more,” you’ll then enter what you’d like to adjust and send the message.
After a few hours, your app’s Home Page will reflect a different set of suggestions.
Spotify says the feature can be used when you want to explore a new genre or era, but aren’t sure where to start, or if you want to adjust the vibe of the music — like if you want more energizing tracks. You can also tell Spotify what sort of podcasts and audiobooks you want to better shape those recommendations.
The feature is still in beta. The company didn’t offer a timeline as to when it would reach a wider audience.

articles.title_zh: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices.
Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week.
What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”.
Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.
Follow UN proceedings live today here.
Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas.
John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”.
Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump.
Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells
A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July.
Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day.
Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose
Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16.
Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

articles.title_orig: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
articles.title_zh: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
articles.content_orig:
Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
KATHMANDU, Nepal — On a recent September day, Sumana Shrestha Amatya stood alongside other protesters in the Nepali capital, urging the government to work faster to find their loved ones, trapped inside hydropower plants since flash floods devastated miles of a river valley in late August.
Amatya says she hasn't heard from officials about her husband, Sunil, a geologist. Still, she acknowledged the scale of the disaster that the government was grappling with: "It was like a Himalayan tsunami."
It's a description other Nepalis have used for the events of Aug. 26, when a glacier and its bedrock spanning more than 3,800 feet in width collapsed into a river valley, some 4,000 feet below.
That triggered 30-foot-high waves of boulders, water and ice that surged for miles downstream. It swept away a multistory border building and some 70 bridges and miles of highway, and buried 12 hydropower plants under mud and boulders along the Trishuli River, which was badly impacted by the floods.
Some 1,400 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, and more than 5,000 remain unaccounted for.
The dead and missing include 121 people who were trapped in hydropower plants, according to Brig. Gen. Subas Jung Thapa of the Nepali army, which is leading rescue efforts. He spoke in early September.
It took days just to find the power plants under the mud. It was like "a bomb's gone off," said Arnold Dix, a tunneling expert helping with rescue efforts. "It's removed the power stations from the surface, like they're just not there." Only three men were found alive in the plants since rescue efforts began.
Did hydropower projects add to the risk?
It is those hydropower plants that have received the most scrutiny in regional media since the floods, with experts reviving questions about whether developers had properly assessed the risks of building them in the Himalayas.
"We need to understand what is happening now in Nepal can happen in other parts of the Himalayas," says C.P. Rajendran, an Indian geoscientist who has been critical of big construction works in the Himalayas. (Rajendran, like many Indians, uses initials for his first name.)
Critics have also focused on the role of international institutions like the World Bank, which has long supported some of these hydropower projects and their associated dams.
They include one of the biggest hydropower projects in the river basin, known as the Upper Trishuli-1, which cost Nepal over half a billion dollars. It was backed by about $300 million in loans and equity by two arms of the World Bank.
The Upper-Trishuli-1 was under construction. Now it's under the mud. Thapa of the Nepali army said in his press briefing that he estimated some 50 people were trapped inside. On Wednesday, the Kathmandu Post reported the bodies of five men were recovered from the plant.
"Why did it have to happen in the first place?" asked Parineeta Dandekar, an expert on rivers who has written critically about these projects for the advocacy group South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People.
Dandekar accuses the World Bank of producing a flawed risk assessment report for the project from the get-go. Its many omissions, Dandekar says, included ignoring "the cumulative disaster risk that can happen after having so many projects across the same river."
Experts say the Trishuli river basin has 36 hydro power projects — including the dozen now under the mud.
Dandekar says the constant blasting of mountains to build these projects, including for miles-long tunnels, has its own impact.
It's a region where earthquakes and landslides are common, and where climate change is causing its glaciers to melt more rapidly, making them — and their slopes — more unstable. Initial analysis suggests global warming exacerbated the melting of the glacier that snapped off in August, triggering flash floods.
There's no clear evidence that the construction of these projects had a role in causing the severity of the Aug. 26 disaster. But experts like geoscientist Rajendran say construction has caused damage in other communities where hydropower projects are being built, including damaging mountain springs, causing homes to crack and even landslides.
In this case, though, says Dipak Gyawali, a hydropower engineer with the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology, "compared to the tectonic forces at play that caused this event, dynamiting is minuscule. This is almost nothing. It's like scratching your skin."
But he and other experts said developers were not seriously investigating the risk caused by so many projects built in the same zone. "These risks have to be properly studied and assessed. Unfortunately, they have not been," Gyawali said.
Retired Indian ambassador Shyam Saran, who served as the Indian prime minister's special envoy for climate change, says developers typically look at risks that could be triggered by their project, alongside environmental risks to it, and they appear safe. "But if you do actually a cumulative environmental impact assessment of the whole river system," he says, "then a different picture emerges."
And the Trishuli river "is a really high-risk area to build [hydropower] dams, says Austin Lord of the Stimson Center, who works on disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region at the Stimson Center. In events exacerbated by climate change, there's been deadly flooding three years in a row in the Trishuli basin. In 2024, it was extreme rainfall. In 2025, a glacial lake burst. This year, a glacier snapped off.
Days before the August flood, Lord and others authored a paper warning that the area was particularly vulnerable to glacial lakes bursting. "Recurring landslides, and prolonged closures," they wrote, "had all highlighted its vulnerability."
In a statement, the World Bank told NPR that the hydropower plant's design reflected assessments that looked at the risk of flooding and landslides using evidence available when the assessment was made in 2018. The statement said that as more information becomes available about the August floods, "the World Bank Group will consider any implications for risk assessment, monitoring, early warning and emergency response measures in hydropower projects."
Another major funder for the Upper Trishuli-1 was the Asian Development Bank, which loaned $60 million for the project. In 2024, independent experts who visited the site reported that no climate resilience assessment was undertaken. They described that as a "significant gap." The bank did not immediately respond to NPR's question as to whether that assessment was ultimately undertaken.
Arnold Dix, the tunneling expert, defended the hydropower plants' construction. "They were built properly to start with," he said, noting the underground infrastructure, including tunnels, was still intact. He said the collapsing glacier that triggered the August flash floods was an unforeseen new threat that "will change the way we do the designs of the power station."
Rethinking hydropower in the Himalayas
Advocates say they hope this devastating flood might prompt a rethink of how hydropower is constructed across the Himalayas. Reuters reported in 2025 that China and India, the world's most populous countries, have built 68 major dams in the Himalayas and another 101 are in the pipeline.
Most prominently, China is constructing one of the world's largest dams and hydropower plants in Tibet, costing around $170 billion. It's estimated that it will provide power to 300 million people.
In July, Chinese geologists reported that the dam is being constructed over an active fault line, risking the integrity of the project's infrastructure. Chinese officials have maintained that the project is safe and that they had considered downstream communities.
"If something happens, it is going to be a monumental disaster," says retired ambassador Saran. He says Chinese authorities have assured their neighbors that the hydro project is safe

articles.title_orig: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.title_zh: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access.
The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing.
It contends that the three news outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ attorney Michael Velchik.
The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes. The letters cite a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
The letters also mention news stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia.
The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims.
The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say.
Rubio defends White House media outlet ban
The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.”
He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated.
First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds.
Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN.
On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” let journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico back into the White House if a court rules against his decision to ban the media outlets from the White House grounds.
Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual.
The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities.
Pool coverage is a decades-old system in which one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
Print and radio pools are still in place, and TV pools for events for other parts of the administration will continue. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

articles.title_orig: Meta says its Muse AI agent can do things for you. I put it to the test
articles.title_zh: Meta says its Muse AI agent can do things for you. I put it to the test
articles.content_orig:
It’s been a busy afternoon for Pip, the AI agent I’ve been using in Meta’s Muse app.
The agent, which Meta launched on September 8, booked a Friday date night and made a packing schedule for my upcoming move. It also emailed a friend about a trip next month and made a planning document with places we want to visit.
A Pixar-like avatar typed away on a laptop at the top of the screen to let me know my AI helper, whose name I chose, was hard at work.
Chatbots like ChatGPT have changed the way people find information and get answers to questions. Now, tech giants are attempting to develop AI assistants that can handle complex tasks, with the goal being that a user can give a broad command like “order my groceries for the week” and go about their day.
Muse is currently the most popular free app in the iPhone’s App Store and has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. It is Meta’s latest and most promising attempt to rival popular chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to share more about his vision for Muse and the company’s AI plans during its Connect conference on Wednesday.
Perhaps most importantly, there’s the question of whether people will trust Meta with even more personal details: Muse’s rise in the App Stores comes after the company’s smart glasses stirred controversy and privacy concerns.
“While feedback (around Muse) has been positive, privacy and trust remain key considerations for broader adoption,” Bank of America analysts wrote in a research note Tuesday.
Muse has more guidance for users compared to ChatGPT or Gemini, which can feel like a blank canvas.
The Muse app has five tabs: the main chat for communicating with the agent, a customizable feed of your interests and priorities, an Ideas tab with prompt examples, a list of goals to track based on previous conversations, and a section for files and media.
For my upcoming move to a new apartment, I told Muse what I still needed to pack, how much time I had before moving and that I wanted to pack in short spurts.
The AI agent made a list of what to pack each day this week, along with how much time I should spend on packing each day. It also gave general tips like setting aside a specific bag for the first night in my new apartment with all my essentials.
Like other AI agents, it’s good at planning-oriented tasks that usually require some combination of Googling, communicating with friends or family and booking reservations.
After connecting my Google apps to Muse, I instructed the agent to email a friend about what she had in mind for our trip to Cape May, New Jersey, next month. When she responded, I had Muse package her restaurant recommendations into a polished Google Doc, along with similar alternative options.
One thing that impressed me was Muse’s ability to understand and communicate roadblocks in tasks. When I had trouble purchasing a bottle of shampoo, it scanned the website to find out why. (It turns out the store it was trying to buy from was a beauty supply store that requires a professional license number).
Muse uses a virtual computer in the cloud for tasks like these, meaning it’s actually browsing the web to accomplish its assigned job. You can see it navigating websites and jump in at any time.
Still, other AI agents like ChatGPT and Gemini can handle similar tasks and sometimes provided more detailed responses.
Things that were easier to do on my own
Muse also served as a reminder that AI isn’t ready to handle everything. When I asked for a list of places to go for date night, it pulled up two options in my neighborhood that had been closed for years.
In one instance, Muse seemed to exaggerate its capabilities.
In its list of prompt ideas, Muse said it could haggle on Facebook Marketplace: “When the right one lands I message the seller, talk the price down against comparable listings, and lock in a time and place,” the app’s Ideas tab said.
But when I tried this, Muse said it couldn’t message sellers directly. It would instead vet the listings and draft a message for me to send to negotiate a lower price.
A Meta spokesperson said the description in the prompt ideas list is accurate and that Muse can negotiate with sellers under parameters set by the user.
Shopping is also often easier to do manually, largely because of restrictions that prevent bots from crawling websites. Amazon prevents Muse from browsing its online store, although Meta’s agent can still retrieve product links through search engines.
While Muse was able to browse Target’s website, I still had to enter personal details manually because the retailer blocked autonomous clicks at checkout. (Muse uses Stripe’s Link digital wallet service for purchases, which it says generates a one-time use card to prevent your credit card number from being shared.)
Meta and its peers are betting their future on AI agents at a time when consumers are increasingly skeptical of the technology.
Roughly two-thirds of American adults say AI is advancing too quickly, and more Americans predict AI will have a negative impact on society rather than positive, according to a Pew Research Center report from June.
Then there’s the privacy question and whether consumers will trust Meta to manage payment information and access apps on their behalf, especially after the Cambridge Analytica scandal. And it’s not just Meta; 41% of Americans said they have very little or no confidence in large technology companies in a Gallup poll published in July.
“AI agents are often framed as helpful personal assistants, but to live up to their potential they typically need an enormous amount of private data to function,” Miranda Bogen, director of the Center for Democracy & Technology’s AI Governance Lab, told CNN in an email. The fact that agents are designed to take action based on this information means the bar is even higher for safeguards, she added.
Meta said it built Muse to be “safe, secure” and “private” and that it runs on a dedicated cloud-based computer that can’t be accessed by other agents. It also said Muse cannot see a user’s passwords or payment methods.
AI companies claim that AI agents are well-suited for online shopping. But market research firm Gartner found that 64% of consumers said they think AI shopping agents will benefit corporations and brands more than consumers.
And despite Muse’s early App Store success, a survey from research firm Emarketer suggests ChatGPT and Gemini are the most widely used AI assistants in the United States by a long shot. When asked which AI tools they prefer or use the most, 33.7% of respondents said ChatGPT, while 18.2% said Gemini and 4.7% said Meta AI, the firm reported in July.
Still, Muse is Meta’s best chance yet at giving them serious competition. At least for now.
