articles.title_orig: Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
articles.title_zh: Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates soared to the highest level since 2024 last week, causing loan demand to fall back again and more borrowers to opt for riskier loans. Total application volume decreased 1.5% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.12% from 6.97%, with points rising to 0.73 from 0.72, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. That was the lowest level since February 2025. The 30-year fixed loan was 78 basis points, or more than three-quarters of a percentage point lower, at the same time last year.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 1% for the week and were 11% lower year over year. The fall housing market, usually the second busiest compared with spring, is now underway, but real estate agents are already noting a sharp pullback due to higher rates. Buyers and current homeowners are also searching for savings anywhere they can find them, even in riskier, adjustable-rate loans.
"With fixed rates much higher, more borrowers opted for ARMs, with the ARM share reaching 9.8%, as rates for 5/1 ARMs were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed rate loans," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA.
The ARM share of applications the week before last was just 8.4%. During the first years of the pandemic, when rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share was barely 3%. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but will adjust either higher or lower depending on where the market is when that term is up.
Mortgage rates moved slightly lower to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, as the price of oil fell and bond yields moved lower as a result.

articles.title_orig: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.title_zh: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.content_orig:
EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved.
"The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.
"The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added.
Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years.
Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable."
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
"Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list".
Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs.
France and Luxembourg sought exemptions
France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list.
Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details.
According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov.
Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg.
Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions.
Who are Usamov and Friedman?
Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion, respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin.
The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators.
For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank.
Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions.
If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

articles.title_orig: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.title_zh: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.content_orig:
Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
Platform adds alternative methods that do not require video selfies or ID to verify age
Discord has re-launched its age verification process for all users, introducing alternative methods that do not require video selfies or ID.
In an update posted yesterday, Discord co-founder and chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy stated that users can verify their age using credit cards, the Apple App Store, Google Play Store, Google Wallet, or AgeKey (which does not share personal or private data).
"By launching a global approach with non-biometric options, we're getting ahead of laws that might ask us to implement something less privacy-focused," said Vishnevskiy.
"The decisions policymakers make now will shape how platforms advance both teen safety and privacy for years to come, and I encourage people to make their perspectives heard where they live."
In February, Discord announced that age verification would be required for all users starting in March.
The rollout was postponed to the second half of 2026 due to privacy concerns. At the time, Vishnevskiy acknowledged that Discord "should have provided more detail about [its] intentions and how the process works."
In its latest update, Discord said it would "publicly document every third-party age assurance vendor and make it clear who each vendor is," which it has done since and can be accessed here.
Discord has also published its age group estimation methodology and released its first age assurance data in the 2026 Transparency Report, which includes information from the UK and Australia launches.
"Previously, I said trust is earned through actions, not posts," said Vishnevskiy. "This launch is where you hold us to that. We'll get some things wrong, but you can judge us on how we respond: how accurate the age group estimation gets, how fast we fix bad calls, and whether we keep publishing the data so you don't have to take my word for it. That's how we earn your trust."
Discord's age verification automatically assigns users to an age group based on account age or associated servers. It does not review messages, calls, or other content.
There are three age groups: Adult (18+), Teen (13 to 17), and Unconfirmed.
New accounts are automatically unconfirmed until Discord has enough data to determine an age group. Users who do not verify their age can continue to use Discord with limitations while the platform determines a group to place them in, though they can verify their age in user settings.

articles.title_orig: Hayden Panettiere Died From Toxic Effects of Fentanyl, Other Drugs
articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere Died From Toxic Effects of Fentanyl, Other Drugs
articles.content_orig:
Hayden Panettiere‘s cause of death has been revealed.
The actress died last month at age 36 from the toxic effects of fentanyl as well as prescription drugs, including alprazolam, known by its brand name Xanax; methocarbamol, a muscle relaxant; and quetiapine, an antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder.
The manner of death was ruled to be an accident, according to the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, which announced its findings early Tuesday.
An autopsy discovered no signs of trauma.
As previously reported, Panettiere was found unresponsive in a Greenville, South Carolina, residence, with first responders and EMS responding to a cardiac arrest. Resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful, and she was pronounced dead.
Panettiere, who began acting as a child, had been open about her struggles with substance abuse, revealing in 2022 that she spent years battling an addiction to opioids and alcohol.
“My saving grace is that I couldn’t be messy while on set and working,” she told People magazine at the time. “But things kept getting out of control [off set]. And as I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn’t live without.”
After welcoming daughter Kaya with ex Wladimir Klitschko, the Heroes and Nashville star struggled with postpartum depression, which she sought treatment for but continued to struggle with drinking and using opioids as her relationship with Klitschko crumbled.
“He didn’t want to be around me,” she said. “I didn’t want to be around me. But with the opiates and alcohol, I was doing anything to make me feel happy for a moment. Then I’d feel worse than I did before. I was in a cycle of self-destruction.”
Later, in an interview on Jay Shetty’s On Purpose podcast timed to the release of her memoir last May, which received renewed attention after her death, Panettiere explained how her postpartum struggles affected her use of drugs and alcohol.
“I never felt any hostility or negativity toward my child, thankfully, but I wasn’t connecting with her the way that I knew I should be, and I was full of stress and anxiety all the time,” Panettiere said. “That’s why I turned to substances — because [of] the anxiety that I started having, the panic attacks that I started having,”
She added, recalling how she’d long wanted to be a mom: “I had this beautiful plan in my head, and then I had my daughter, and I knew something was just terribly, terribly wrong. I was miserable. I was in tears all the time. Even though the alcohol helped my nervous system calm down, it is a depressant, so over time it made things worse, not better.”
Panettiere was in Greenville, South Carolina with her on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson, both of whom called 911, according to a heavily redacted incident report from the Greenville Police Department.
When paramedics arrived, Brian Hickerson showed them a “bag of medication” he said she had been taking, according to the police report.
Zach Hickerson later told TMZ that Brian gave Panettiere Narcan, a medication used to reverse the effects of an opioid overdose.
Just days after Panettiere died, the Drug Enforcement Administration reportedly joined the investigation into her death.
Last week, TMZ reported that Panettiere died from taking a pill laced with fentanyl.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi meeting: Why China's self-sufficiency changes the calculus
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi meeting: Why China's self-sufficiency changes the calculus
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The trade deficit that escalated tensions between China and the U.S. in recent years has yet to shrink significantly, and the world's second-largest economy faces deep challenges. But China's efforts to build up self-sufficiency have reduced the threat to its domestic market from global trade developments.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet this week for their second in-person summit of the year. U.S. concerns about artificial intelligence have gained prominence in the days ahead of the meeting.
But the best that businesses are hoping for is an extension of a trade truce reached last fall. Even then, tariffs have done little to dent America's appetite for Chinese goods.
While an escalation in trade tensions last April briefly sent the U.S. trade deficit with China to its lowest level since 2017, surging demand for AI-related parts have helped send it higher again so far this year, according to China Customs data accessed through Wind Information.
And even as the U.S. has diversified away from China, it's hard for the world to shake its dependence on the Asian country.
Asia still accounts for more than 60% of U.S. imports, the same as before "Liberation Day," pointed out Jens Eskelund, president of the European Chamber of Commerce in China.
He estimated between half and three-quarters of container traffic from China to Southeast Asia subsequently heads on to other destinations.
That's all sped up the pace at which the world relies on China-made goods.
Eskelund said he previously expected China to account for 40% of global container exports in the year 2030 — but the milestone was reached this summer.
How did the world get here?
"Probably the China shock only really started in 2022, because I think everything was distorted by the pandemic," Eskelund said. "China was first in the pandemic, and first out of the pandemic, and for that reason China actually could allow its exchange rate to rise, and export prices to rise.
"China could do that because China was the only game in town," he said.
China's real estate market began its downturn in 2022, dragging down domestic demand. Chinese companies ramped up global expansion, and exports.
"There is a direct, perfect correlation between the drop in export prices and the acceleration in export in volume terms," Eskelund said.
U.S. tech companies' buildout of data centers to power AI has supported demand for Chinese goods.
But think tank CF40 estimated that for the first time this year, AI-related exports fell significantly in August from a year ago.
Macquarie's chief China economist Larry Hu last week also pointed out that the recent performance of the PHLX Semiconductor Index — which he said tends to be predictive of how China's high-tech exports will grow in the next six months — "does not bode well for China's export outlook over the next year."
Still, economists don't expect China's policymakers to do much.
Within tech-related manufacturing, industrial robot output rose by 34.6% year-on-year in August, while smartphone output fell by 22.3%.
"Because there are always high-flying subsectors for the government to point to, policymakers do not appear to feel much urgency to introduce additional easing measures, absent a sharp deterioration in the labor market," Goldman Sachs' chief China economist Hui Shan said in a Sept. 20 report.
She pointed out house prices have already seen a 30% decline over a six-year timeline, typical of historical large-scale property downturns in other parts of the world. "Weak labor markets and still-falling rents are likely to prolong the downturn in many parts of China," she added.
The number of loss-making companies is also on the rise, accounting for 24% of industrial firms in China in 2025.
The economic slowdown has only pushed companies in China to compete even more fiercely with each other, and their foreign rivals.
The American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai said this month that three-quarters of members responding to a survey saw Chinese rivals as more advanced, and that the perceived gap in product quality narrowed by 6 percentage points from last year.
For the first time since 2022, domestic competition has surpassed geopolitical tensions as the top challenge for members, the chamber said.
It's all spilling over internationally, as European Union officials are starting to follow the U.S. in scrutiny of China-origin exports. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, who urged "tangible results" from China on trade by October, is expected to travel to Beijing next month.
The European Union has the largest trade deficit with China of any economy, Eskelund pointed out.
In addition to competing through lower-cost goods, Chinese companies have also come to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals. This also supports Beijing's self-sufficiency goals.
"There's no sense in which China's strategy seems to be at all dependent on actions that the rest of the world might take," said Chad Bown, senior fellow at the U.S.-based Peterson Institute for International Economics.
It's "this strategy of a one-way dependence of the rest of the world on China that it's going to weaponize."
—CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s midterm woes deepen amid worsened economic backdrop: CNN poll
articles.title_zh: Trump’s midterm woes deepen amid worsened economic backdrop: CNN poll
articles.content_orig:
With President Donald Trump at record unpopularity, Republicans are facing an even bleaker midterm political landscape than they did eight years ago, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds.
Nationally, voters say they prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by an eight-point margin – slightly more modest than their 12-point advantage in CNN’s September polling ahead of the 2018 midterms in Trump’s first presidency.
But Trump is even more unpopular than he was in 2018, and the economic backdrop has worsened considerably. In his first term, Trump saw net-positive ratings on the economy, which Americans largely saw as thriving. Now, just 27% of Americans approve of Trump on the economy, down 22 points from 2018. And 28% call economic conditions good – a drop of 41 points.
The issue has risen in prominence: Two-thirds of registered voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, higher than in the autumn before either of the past two midterms. And, in a shift from recent trends, Americans say they agree more with Democrats than Republicans when it comes to the issue.
That leaves a midterm electorate in which the president’s supporters are largely tepid, while his opponents are furious. In a midterm high for an incumbent president dating back to the George W. Bush era, 44% of registered voters say they view their congressional vote as a message of opposition to Trump. Just 19%, by contrast, say their vote will be a message of support for the president.
At the same time, the public remains split on what a Democratic congressional victory might mean for the cost of living in the US, or their own financial situation.
Support for Trump continues to erode
Overall, just one-third of Americans now approve of Trump’s job performance, the continuation of a steady decline throughout his second term. That’s on par with the 34% he saw in July, but marks a numeric low in either term of his presidency.
Only 13% now say they strongly approve of his performance, another career low. Just 24% say he has the right priorities, and a scant 20% approve of his handling of inflation.
Two-thirds of Americans say Trump has worsened economic conditions in the country, and majorities say that the war in Iran, as well as new tariffs, have had a negative effect on their own finances. By contrast, few say they’re seeing benefits from Trump policies like changes to the tax law, or the establishment of Trump Accounts for children born during his second term. Most Americans also call increased gas prices a financial hardship for their household – and though only about one-quarter call that hardship severe, the public remains dubious that Trump has any plan to address the issue.
A 57% majority of Americans say they feel uncertain about their own finances, with nearly half expressing stress about their financial future – a sentiment that’s particularly acute among younger adults. Just 31% of Americans say they feel hope and 23% that they feel security, down 8 and 7 points respectively from spring. More than one-third aren’t confident about maintaining their current standard of living, worse than the numbers at the tail end of the Great Recession.
While Republicans haven’t deserted Trump, relatively few remain enthusiastic about the current state of his presidency. Only 35% say they strongly approve of him, down from 66% in September 2018. In the latest poll, 50% of Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, 59% say the Iran war has hurt their finances, and nearly half say he’s worsened or had no effect on economic conditions.
Democrats are fired up for the midterm, but the public’s expectations for a Democratic Congress aren’t high
Overall, voters say, 49% to 41%, that they’d support a Democratic candidate over a Republican candidate in their congressional district. Democratic and Democratic-leaning registered voters are 16 points likelier than GOP-aligned voters to say they’re extremely motivated to vote this year.
Among the full public, anger at Trump and deep dissatisfaction with the status quo are paired with real skepticism about the prospects of a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Both congressional Democrats and congressional Republicans are deeply – and about equally – unpopular, with about one-quarter of Americans approving.
And while Americans say by a 10-point margin that a Democratic-controlled Congress would have a positive effect on health care policy, they’re closely split on whether a change in power would be more positive or negative when it comes to the cost of living in the US, their own finances, corruption, or foreign policy.
But the Democrats are nevertheless seen as the lesser of two evils on a crucial issue: They lead the GOP by 7 points as the party Americans say is closest to their own views on the economy. Over the past four years, this is both by far the best number for Democrats and the worst for Republicans on the topic.
A 68% majority of voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, topping a list of more than 10 issues. That’s far higher than the 59% in fall 2022 or 44% in fall 2018 who called the issue extremely important.
The poll finds that elections themselves, election integrity and voting rights are also at the forefront of many partisans’ minds as Trump continues his efforts to reshape or cast doubt on parts of the voting system, with 61% calling the issue extremely important. Majorities also say that inflation and health care are extremely important, while other hot-button issues – including data centers and AI, abortion, and policies around gender identity and trans people – don’t register as deeply.
Voters’ decisions, though, aren’t always down to which issues they find most important – more than half of voters say that other factors will be more important in their vote for Congress this year. And in this year where discontent with Washington is at the forefront of many voters’ minds, about a third say their votes will be primarily driven by which party will control the House of Representatives, including almost 4 in 10 of the most motivated voters.
CNN’s Jennifer Agiesta, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS online and by telephone September 16-17 among a random national sample of 1,206 adults, including 867 registered voters. Results for the full sample have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points; it is 4.1 points among registered voters.

articles.title_orig: Poll: Canadians and Americans agree, Trump was in the wrong with trade war
articles.title_zh: Poll: Canadians and Americans agree, Trump was in the wrong with trade war
articles.content_orig:
It’s become an article of faith for trade hardliners in both parties that a protectionist agenda is a guaranteed pathway to building support among working-class voters. But now that President Donald Trump is testing that theory in practice, it is largely flopping on the campaign trail.
Trump has pursued the most confrontational trade agenda of any president since at least William McKinley at the end of the 19th century, and by the estimation of some historians, even Thomas Jefferson around its beginning.
But even in heavily blue-collar states and House districts that were long believed to be the most receptive to a protectionist agenda, Democrats almost uniformly have been comfortable this year running against the Trump tariffs, while Republicans have struggled to defend them. Even Democrats who are deeply skeptical of free trade agreements — like Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and Brian Poindexter, the ironworker running against Rep. Max Miller for an Ohio House seat — have been unreserved in condemning the Trump tariffs. Polls by CNN and other media organizations consistently show that far more Americans believe the tariffs have hurt rather than helped their financial bottom line — and that consensus extends even to working-class white voters without a four-year college degree.
All this marks a fundamental shift in the politics of trade that could loosen Trump’s hold on the working-class voters at the core of his coalition — and allow Democrats this fall to recover some of the ground they have lost in blue-collar and rural places. Trump’s skepticism about the North American Free Trade Agreement and other moves to lower trade barriers clearly helped power his historic gains in blue-collar communities during his initial 2016 race and his first presidential term. But his sweeping second-term tariffs — which exceed even the wish lists that other protectionist presidential candidates have put forward since the 1970s — appear to be bleeding Republican support, even in those working-class places. “Everyone else talked about it, but Trump did it,” says Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the American Action Forum, a center-right think tank. “And voters are like: ‘no thanks.’”
The most protectionist president in modern history
For decades, a steady procession of presidential hopefuls in both parties had offered a tough-on-trade message and an assortment of policies to restrict imports. That list extends from Republican John Connally in 1980 to Democrats Walter Mondale and Richard Gephardt in the 1980s to GOP insurgent Patrick J. Buchanan and independent candidate Ross Perot in the 1990s.
But before Trump, none of them won the presidency — and with it the ability to implement a protectionist agenda. Presidents of both parties have often provided some protection to American industries threatened by foreign competitors. But the general pattern since Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1930s has been that Republican and Democratic presidents alike have generally defended free trade, while the protectionist impulse has been confined mostly to Congress, notes Douglas Irwin, an economics professor at Dartmouth College and historian of American trade policy.
Trump’s willingness to impose tariffs on a panoramic list of US trading partners is unmatched since McKinley in the 1890s, says Alan Tonelson, a longtime manufacturing trade policy analyst and advocate for import restrictions. Irwin thinks Trump outmatches even McKinley: He believes Trump is pursuing the most confrontational trade policy since Jefferson imposed an (ultimately disastrous) 1807 embargo on all commerce with both England and Napoleon-era France in protest of their attacks on American shipping during their worldwide conflict. “There’s been no president in modern history who has used the tariff threat nearly as much as Donald Trump,” says Irwin.
Stanley Greenberg, a longtime Democratic pollster who has studied the party’s diminishing support among working-class white voters since the 1980s, says that Trump’s hardline approach on trade contributed to his 2016 breakthroughs against Hillary Clinton in battered blue-collar communities that had, in many cases, previously voted for Barack Obama during his two presidential victories.
“Hillary got hurt and Obama got hurt by not understanding these sentiments in the industrial Midwest,” Greenberg says. “And Trump used that to his advantage to win the election in 2016 and it was a fundamental part of his presidency in the first term, in which the association of him going after bad trade agreements and him championing tariffs” allowed him to present himself as a champion of “forgotten” working-class voters.
In his first term, Trump sharply veered from the preponderantly free trade outlook of his three immediate predecessors: Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton. Trump renegotiated NAFTA, the free trade agreement that Clinton pushed through Congress; scrapped the pan-Asian free trade agreement that Obama had negotiated (but never submitted to Congress for fear of hurting Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election); and imposed tariffs primarily on steel and aluminum imports from many countries as well as a wide array of products from China.
But all that was barely an overture for Trump’s second term. To a far greater extent than in his first term, Trump has levied, withdrawn and reimposed tariffs; brandished threats; and launched investigations in a bewildering blur that has upended the rules of trade with dozens of countries. He has moved as aggressively against allies, such as Canada and the European Union, as against traditional trade adversaries such as China.
Before Trump, Holtz-Eakin notes, many political leaders believed “the politics were good” for protectionism, “but the foreign policy implications were bad.” As a result, “no Republican would go there,” he says. “But Trump didn’t care about the latter. So, we’ve (been able) to see the economics in isolation.” And the reaction has been very different than what Trump — and other trade hawks — expected.
Tariffs seemed more popular in theory than they are in practice
Since at least the 1970s, the dominant assumption in each party has been that trade issues divided the public along educational lines, with college-educated voters the most likely to favor expanding trade and working-class voters most receptive to a protectionist message of restricting imports to try to protect domestic manufacturing jobs.
That traditional divide persisted even as Trump returned to office. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ annual foreign policy polling, for instance, found that in 2025 nearly two-thirds of whites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that imposed restrictions on imports to protect jobs over an approach that minimized restrictions to lower prices. Whites with a college degree split evenly over which approach they preferred; notably, however, in a sharp departure from their white counterparts, a slight majority of nonwhites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that focused on costs. College-educated nonwhites were the most skeptical of all toward restrictions.
But as Trump has implemented his tariffs, they have proven less attractive for most Americans in practice than in theory. In Pew polling this January, 60% of Americans opposed his tariff increases; more than twice as many said it had affected their family negatively as positively. In a CNN/SSRS poll this April, four times as many Americans said the tariffs had hurt their personal finances as said they’d helped. Recent polls in Wisconsin and Ohio, two heavily working-class, manufacturing-oriented states, both found about 60% of residents opposed the tariffs. Polls released this month have found overwhelming opposition to Trump’s latest trade war against Canada, particularly in states along the border: In CNN surveys, about two-thirds or more of voters in both Michigan and Maine said the new Canadian tariffs were bad for their state.
I

articles.title_orig: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.title_zh: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.content_orig:
The year’s not nearly over, but 2026 has already delivered a glut of exciting Android phones. Still, we can’t help but think about what might come next. Every phone-maker has distinct ideas about what features they’d like to add and improve with every generation. Some of these things, like design, they can do alone, but others require close collaboration with their partners.
Two such partners are Google and Qualcomm – the former on the software side and the latter on the hardware side. Every summer at Google I/O, we learn about a slew of new software features that will enhance existing and upcoming Android phones. Then, every fall, Qualcomm, which makes the chips, gives us a glimpse of what power and features those companies, like Samsung and Motorola, will have to play with in upcoming releases.
On Tuesday at the Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced a pair of powerful new chips – the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.
“We’re just now at the beginning of the agentic age, and Snapdragon is the platform built for it,” added Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, in his Snapdragon Summit keynote.
Of the new dual chips, it’s the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 that will really take phones to the next level of performance and AI capabilities. The chip “represents the pinnacle of Snapdragon innovation, purpose-built for the most advanced AI workloads and the experiences that will define the agentic era,” said Qualcomm product marketing manager Charlie Beeman in a briefing ahead of the announcement.
The Extreme sees inevitable improvements to speed, connectivity and efficiency, but more interesting are the tweaks Qualcomm has made to enable new experiences and features that it simply wasn’t possible to include on prior Android phones.
“It brings an enormous amount of compute power to a smartphone, and therefore opens up a lot of new opportunities in terms of the applications that could be developed,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. “But it’s a bit of a chicken and egg situation because until that’s enabled on the phones, we won’t know what those applications are going to be.”
A question mark lingers over how different phone-makers will tap the power of the Elite Extreme, but Qualcomm has given us some distinct areas where we can expect to see new experiences. Here are three to look out for and look forward to.
“How’s the camera?” is pretty much the first question everyone will ask when coming across a new smartphone in the wild. Phone-makers know that image quality and camera capabilities are priorities for any new device, and while a lot of that comes down to choices made by the manufacturer, Qualcomm chips still run the show when it comes to the phone’s imaging pipeline.
Both of the new Snapdragon chips will enable a refined camera experience with intelligent stabilization and every pixel now carrying 16 bits of data. The image signaling processor is also tightly coupled to the NPU, a specialized chip that accelerates AI and machine learning tasks. This will enable AI to work on an image while it’s being captured, instead of after. This allows for a dramatic leap in raw throughput and professional-grade video, and a far deeper understanding of every pixel in your scene.
“Each element of the scene is processed individually, helping ensure every shot looks natural, consistent, and remarkably true to life,” said Lekha Motiwala, Qualcomm’s senior director of product management, speaking at Snapdragon Summit.
And the Extreme version of the chip offers more capabilities, such as enabling phone cameras to record video in 8K resolution at 60 fps or film in 4K resolution at 240 fps for super-slow-mo footage.
“You’ll see this coming for the first time in Snapdragon-powered smartphones,” said Motiwala. “It’s not just about getting a shot. It’s about preserving a moment as you experienced it.”
There’s simply no way for AI to be personal without it really getting to know you. Agentic AI that lacks personal context – past, present and future – would be like speaking with a different stranger each time you pick up your phone.
The 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is engineered to collect that context, hold onto it and draw from it whenever needed. This is all thanks to Qualcomm’s new Sensing Hub, which, with its dual micro-NPUs, can support models up to 200 million parameters. The company’s updated Personal Scribe can then remember who said what, why it matters and learn from your messages, emails and conversations to build your private knowledge graph.
It could expand an AI agent’s ability to give you nuanced answers to questions, help you recall when and to whom you made specific promises, and make future plans for you based on a whole range of factors, such as your availability, schedule, travel preferences and need for relaxation or concentrated working time.
With its ability to run over 30 billion different models on device, the Elite Extreme Gen 6 is definitely leading the way when it comes to running agentic AI. “When you have this level of capability, your work starts before you even open your inbox,” said Amon. “Here, an agent digests your [Snapdragon] Summit invitation, understands the dates, the flights, the venue details, key moments inside it, and it builds a plan.”
Phones can be overlooked as gaming devices, but for Qualcomm, providing a best-in-class mobile gaming experience remains a priority.
With the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 2, the company is introducing an AI-rendering technology called Adreno Neural Fusion, which is supported across major game engines, including Unreal, Unity and Messiah. It can deliver upscaled images with “rock-solid frame rates” at lower power, according to Matthew Grossman, manager of product marketing at Qualcomm.
Adreno Neural Fusion is “a proprietary technology designed by Qualcomm from the ground up, not an off-the-shelf implementation,” said Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of handsets. “It’s a tightly integrated architecture that brings graphics and AI together to knock a new class of intelligent gaming experiences.”
In addition, AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores run advanced models, and the chip features 18MB of high-performance memory. So what does this mean for your mobile gaming experience? The answer is better picture quality, higher frame rates and longer play times with games drawing less power than in the past. It’s a win-win-win.

articles.title_orig: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.title_zh: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.content_orig:
Gable Steveson has broken his silence following the stunning first loss of his professional MMA career.
Steveson released a lengthy statement Tuesday through his manager, Abraham Kawa, addressing his historic 12-second upset at the hands of Sean Sharaf at UFC 331. The Olympic champion described the defeat as a "mistake on my end" and vowed to respond much like he did following setbacks during his decorated amateur wrestling career.
"Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same," Steveson wrote. "I will be great, and this won't deny me."
Steveson also addressed the allegations of sexual assault stemming from a 2019 incident in his college years that resurfaced during UFC 331 fight week.
Steveson's full statement can be read below:
— Abe kawa (@Abraham_kawa) September 22, 2026
This statement is for my family, my friends, my fans, and the people who truly know me and know the kind of man I am. I know there are people who will never support me, no matter what I say or do. That's their choice. But I'm speaking to the people who know me, not just as an athlete, but as a husband and a father to a young daughter.
Prior to and during fight week, an incident from my college years was brought up by my opponent. I believe it was raised to get in my head, but it also reopened something that had been addressed years ago.
I want to be clear: I did not do anything alleged. I was never charged with a crime, and the matter was ultimately dropped by the district attorney. The allegations were not ignored nor brushed aside. They were thoroughly and heavily reviewed as I fully cooperated with law enforcement, including a separate Title IX review.
There were no criminal charges, no conviction, and no finding of responsibility against me. The matter was closed, and there is no pending legal issue involving me. My own attorney did their own investigation and stated on the record that even if the law was changed, I would have the same outcome, which now speaks for itself.
I understand how serious allegations like this are, and I understand that people may have questions when they hear only part of a story. Moving forward, I am going to keep focusing on my wife, my daughter, my family, and the work in front of me. To the people who support me, thank you. I know who I am. My family knows who I am. The people who have walked with me through life know who I am. That's what matters to me, and that's where I'm going to keep my focus.
As for my opponent, congratulations. You caught me. A mistake on my end was made. It was your night. Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same. I will be great, and this won't deny me.
Steveson, 26, entered UFC 331 with many hailing him as the most talented heavyweight prospect in recent MMA history. His stunning loss to Sharaf, who held an 0-2 UFC record prior to Saturday night, marked the biggest UFC betting upset of all time for Draft Kings.
Along with being a two-time NCAA Division I national champion as an amateur wrestler and two-time Dan Hodge Trophy winner — the award given annually to collegiate athletics' top freestyle wrestler — Steveson was best known within the wrestling world for his run through the 2020 Olympics, when he stunned the global field at just 21 years old to become the youngest freestyle wrestler in his division to ever win gold.
Entering UFC 331, Steveson was already 4-0 with four first-round knockouts in his first year as a professional MMA fighter, culminating in a two-minute thrashing of Elisha Ellison this past July in his UFC debut. His matchup with Sharaf, however, proved to be different in more ways than one, as the former U.S. Marine made Steveson's 2019 sexual assault allegations a central focus of the bout's pre-fight build.
In June 2019, Steveson and a teammate on the University of Minnesota wrestling team, Dylan Martinez, were arrested on suspicion of sexual assault. The case was ultimately dropped after investigators determined there was "inadequate evidence" to convict the two wrestlers. Prosecutors also pointed to a Minnesota law that limited how sexual assault cases involving intoxicated victims could be charged. That law has since been changed.
In the immediate aftermath of Steveson's loss at UFC 331, the heavyweight prospect fled the cage before the result's official announcement could be read — a decision which drew a flood of criticism. UFC Hall of Famer Daniel Cormier went so far as to lambaste the Olympian for being an "ungrateful loser" on UFC 331's post-fight broadcast.
UFC legend Jon Jones, who has served as one of Steveson's primary mentors and coaches, has since said it was his decision "to take Gable straight to the back after the fight," citing a desire to "get my friend to the back to make sure he was OK."

A federal judge has set a hearing for Thursday on the proposed settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set the hearing for 11 a.m. PT via Zoom.
She wrote in an order Tuesday that the hearing would be to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties proposed consent decree, as well as the implementation of the proposed consent decree.”
The parties have filed a motion to approve the consent decree, which lays out a series of settlement conditions to resolve the lawsuit brought by the state AGs in July. Among the provisions are Paramount commitments to release at least 30 movies per year, and another to create an independent board to oversee CNN and CBS News adherence to journalistic standards.
The judge also canceled a scheduled hearing on whether to require the state AGs to post a bond as the litigation proceeded.
The judge said in a separate order that she would decide in “due course” on whether to dismiss the lawsuit brought by the Writers Guild of America to block the merger. The WGA said it also reached a settlement with Paramount to end its litigation.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.content_orig:
As recently as last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping was expected to arrive in Washington with a large delegation of Chinese CEOs, as President Trump touted a dealmaking atmosphere surrounding the two leaders' summit.
Now, Xi is scheduled to arrive this evening with a significantly smaller business delegation in tow, dampening expectations even as an array of US executives remains set to be on hand for the gathering.
Chinese state media announced Xi's departure for the US on Wednesday, noting only a small entourage that included family members and political aides.
The South China Morning Post reported that a lack of progress on deals had led to the paring back of the list from the Chinese side.
US industry leaders had been expecting a wide array of Chinese business leaders to be in attendance from electric car makers and agriculture companies.
A White House official didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Trump's team previously confirmed Thursday's state dinner would include Sam Altman of OpenAI (OPAI.PVT), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA).
The summit is set to begin this evening, when Trump will travel to Joint Base Andrews to greet Xi when he arrives at 6 p.m. ET.
The tone shift around business deals comes as other policy areas like AI and trade are expected to see only small steps forward, and signs emerge that Trump is set to roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.
Close observers of US-China relations have noted that Xi did not do the same when Trump visited Beijing in May, sending a subordinate for Trump's arrival.
Some of the US CEOs set to attend this week's festivities, including Huang and Musk, traveled with Trump to Beijing earlier this year.
Members of both leaders' economic teams are set to be in attendance, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, who met in New York over the weekend.
Bessent left that meeting describing the talks as constructive and saying the US had proposed a new AI safety "notification mechanism" that could allow Bessent and He and other officials to communicate quickly in the event of an incident related to AI. But China has yet to publicly embrace the idea.
The lack of further progress on AI underscored the modest ambitions of this week's summit that might be high on pomp and circumstance but light on policy.
There is little expectation of the US or China agreeing to broader limits on AI, such as regulating frontier models. In fact, both sides have signaled that they are eager to race forward with the technology.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
articles.title_zh: ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
articles.content_orig:
ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
“The CCP’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price.”
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senator Ted Budd (R-N.C.) delivered remarks on the Senate floor yesterday ahead of President Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping of the People’s Republic of China. In his speech, Senator Budd called attention to China’s war on religious freedom, its role in fueling the U.S. drug epidemic, its relationship with key U.S. adversaries, and the consequential state of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) race.
Watch Senator Budd’s remarks:
Read Senator Budd’s remarks, as prepared for delivery:
This week, President Xi Jinping will visit the U.S. for bilateral meetings at a pivotal moment for U.S.-China relations. During his two terms in office, President Trump has been clear that under his leadership, the United States must engage with China given the reality of our economic relationship, but we can’t forget that China is also a competitor and an adversary.
The Chinese Communist Party’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price. America’s economy, our fundamental values, and our security—both at home and abroad—have been challenged by the CCP.
I’ve long believed a whole-of-government approach is necessary to address this, and I am grateful that President Donald Trump is at the helm for these crucial negotiations.
China is our most consequential geopolitical competitor, and we cannot afford to ignore the CCP’s ambitions to reorganize global order at the expense of the United States or underestimate the CCP’s rapidly progressing hard and soft power influence around the world to execute this goal.
When President Xi enters the White House later this week, I hope discussions between our two nations include America’s most fundamental values and responsibilities upfront: the protection of American citizens abroad and reiterating a zero-tolerance for violating the God-given right to religious freedom. Let me be clear: there is no excuse for the CCP to unjustly target American citizens abroad or their families, harass religious groups, or carry out a broad-sweeping war on faith in China.
To this day, eight leaders of Zion Church remain behind bars in China because of China’s attack on religious freedom. These detainments are egregious and cannot be ignored. China’s persecution of Christians and other religious groups must not go unaddressed. This is why, during my time in the Senate, I’ve sought to implement strict sanctions on any CCP official who is responsible for or directly carries out violations of religious freedom.
Under President Trump’s leadership, we have already proven to China that the United States has zero tolerance for religious persecution, and we have seen notable results.
At the U.S.-China Summit this past May, President Trump personally raised the case of Zion Church Pastor Ezra Jin with President Xi. Two months later, Pastor Jin was released and returned to U.S. soil, where he was reunited with his family after years of unjust detention. While we are deeply grateful for Pastor Jin’s return, we must never stop fighting to bring home the numerous pastors still unjustly detained and to defend the freedom to worship around the world.
China’s pattern of wrongfully detaining Americans, or relatives of American citizens, is not limited solely to religious crackdowns. I also want to highlight the bipartisan effort Senator Markey and I have taken to bring home both Dr. Youlin Chen and Mr. Min Zin, American academics currently being held in brutal and inhumane conditions.
I am grateful for this body’s bicameral, bipartisan support in condemning the People’s Republic of China’s repeated pattern of arbitrary or wrongful detention of United States citizens.
Here at home, China’s influence and key role in the illicit drug supply chain have resulted in the loss of far too many American lives, the destruction of families, and stolen livelihoods.
I’ve met with far too many families changed forever by the impacts of the drug epidemic. Through buying up American farmland, malign actors have brought the production of illegal hemp-derived products into our communities, and our children are paying the price. And by partnering with transnational criminal organizations, Chinese-connected companies have intentionally made highly addictive, intoxicating substances—like fentanyl and illicit vapes—readily accessible to Americans.
But make no mistake: China is aware of the consequences of its actions. That is exactly why Beijing has no problem extending law enforcement and counter-narcotics cooperation to other nations to mitigate these outcomes. But Chinese products are still flooding American markets in what looks more and more like a reverse Opium War. It needs to end.
Just last week, the Trump administration listed the PRC as one of 23 major drug-transit and producing countries. We have rightfully planted the flag, and now we must demand action to dismantle this criminal enterprise preying on the American people. Ahead of his meetings, President Trump is right to raise this issue directly with President Xi.
Mister President, the American people cannot be blind to China’s efforts to threaten our national security. Especially since the PRC’s growing economic and strategic relationships with adversaries like Russia, Iran, and North Korea have had sweeping consequences.
Earlier this year, at the U.S.-China summit in Beijing, President Trump and President Xi agreed that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and the Strait of Hormuz must remain open for the free flow of global energy.
But if Beijing wants to maintain a productive relationship with Washington, it must recognize the consequences of continuing to partner with adversarial nations that fundamentally defy U.S. interests on the world stage.
Recent reports suggest that China provided Iran with intelligence, including satellite imagery that led to the death of three American service members.
A PRC State-owned firm has reportedly supplied Russia with materials for kamikaze drones, violating sanctions. And the PRC has reportedly supplied Iran with air defense equipment, among other goods, bypassing sanctions.
This behavior cannot continue.
America’s national security must remain at the center of every discussion shaping the future of U.S.-China relations, including the race to develop technologies that will define this century.
We are in a race with China to develop the next generation of advanced manufacturing technology, quantum computing, space travel and satellite technology, and perhaps most consequentially, artificial intelligence.
China’s cyber-threats to the U.S. government have been well documented and damaging to our government and private sector even before the rise of artificial intelligence.
The AI race is not simply about who builds the most powerful model. It is about who will set the standards, safeguards, and norms that will govern one of the most consequential technologies of our time.
Beijing’s national AI strategy calls for China to reach world-leading levels in artificial intelligence by 2030 and surpass the U.S. That reality should alarm us all—especially given that these models are being developed within fundamentally different political systems.
China is developing and deploying AI within its authoritarian system that employs censorship and state surveillance. In dramatic contrast, our models are being developed under constitutional principles that promote free speech, value individualism, and encourage private enterprise.
As the Senator from North Carolina, a state with a growing tech industry, thriving pharmaceutical manufacturing, a pivotal financial sector, and a critical agriculture industry, my state represents many of the successes the PRC aspires to.

articles.title_orig: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.title_zh: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors.
The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”
One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement.
Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, that called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress, by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots.
China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots.
Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.”
Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November.
Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power.
Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.”
China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship.
But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.
Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers.
“They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary.
China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation.
Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making.
Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran.
When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.”
The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit.
Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.”

articles.title_orig: How the US gave up its edge to China in processing vital rare earth minerals – and what that’s costing
articles.title_zh: How the US gave up its edge to China in processing vital rare earth minerals – and what that’s costing
articles.content_orig:
Look around you, and you’ll see rare earth elements at work. A phone vibrates because a magnet moves a weight. Its screen was polished with cerium powder. Its connection to the rest of the world crosses oceans on cables amplified with erbium. If you drove today, a rare earth magnet helped you steer, and a cerium compound scrubbed the exhaust.
All of these devices function because of 17 metals collectively known as rare earth elements. The scientists who gave the group that name in 1794 created a misnomer. Cerium alone is about as common in the Earth’s crust as copper.
However, separating rare earth minerals from one another and from raw ore is intensely difficult. As a result, countries that control the processing of rare earth minerals have a lot of political leverage.
China processes most of the rare earth minerals used around the world, and it isn’t just consumer electronics that depend on Chinese exports. The U.S. military’s F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines need rare earths too.
I spent years adjudicating war games for the U.S. Navy. War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint.
China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a series of export controls issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend – at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very big stick.
California’s Mountain Pass mine led world production of rare earths until the late 1980s. Multiple instances of radioactive wastewater spilling from the mine into the Mojave Desert made it hard to keep domestic production running.
When China expanded its own mining and sold the processed materials for less, the logic of switching rare earth suppliers was easy.
Mountain Pass’ separation plant closed in 1998, and the mine itself stopped in 2002. MP Materials restarted mining there in 2017 as concern about access to rare earth minerals rose, but the U.S. still imported more than two-thirds of the rare earth elements it used as recently as 2025.
China, which mined about 60% of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about 91% of separation and refining.
Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising.
The U.S. Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years. Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons.
China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the U.S. has far fewer experts. Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023.
The U.S. government has committed more than US$7 billion since April 2025 to try to rebuild U.S. rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought $400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials in 2025, giving it 15% ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028.
The Commerce Department also signed a letter of intent in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma.
But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult.
On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures. One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up 0.1% or more of its value, or if it used Chinese rare earth technology.
After President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping that month, Beijing suspended six export controls until Nov. 10, 2026, in exchange for Washington pausing its “affiliates rule,” which imposes restrictions on companies that are majority-owned by certain blacklisted firms, for one year.
Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses.
Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the heavier rare earths.
Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets – critical to speakers and electrical motors – because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “day to day” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production only with Beijing’s approval.
On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put 10 U.S. companies on its export control list. Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems and military vehicles. Two of them – MP Materials and USA Rare Earth – are the federally backed American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain.
Beijing said its move was a response to a similar move by the Pentagon. My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing.
An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice.
For the U.S., leaving processing in China is the fastest and cheapest solution, but that leaves it exposed to Beijing’s restrictions.
Rebuilding a U.S. rare earths supply chain would remove most U.S. dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars and separation produces acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues.
Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the U.S. being cut off unilaterally. Japan has run this play with some success, but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad.
President Xi’s Sept. 24, 2026, meeting with Trump may help determine the status of the Nov. 10 restrictions, but the larger conflict over leverage will continue.
