articles.title_zh: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.content_orig:
Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team”.
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.
Rodriguez took the reins in Venezuela after the US raided her country’s capital of Caracas and seized Maduro, the toppled autocrat, in the dead of night. Since then, she’s been pliant to US interests and brokered a deal that would see a vast share of her country’s oil wealth into US coffers.
During remarks to reporters, Rubio said that the US was working to “create the groundwork and rebuild the institutions necessary to have free and fair elections in Venezuela.”
But he caveated that free and fair elections would have to wait until Venezuela was in the shape to support an “enduring Republic,” and that its first elected leader could not inherit “a complete catastrophe, economic and social.”
The conditions for such a democratic transition, per Rubio, include rebuilding Venezuela’s independent media, creating the infrastructure for a trustworthy electoral process, and bringing back opposition political parties exiled abroad. Here Rubio name dropped María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who had maintained close tied with Trump before the administration ultimately backed Rodriguez.
Speaking to reporters at the UN, Rubio alludes to regime change in Cuba
Addressing reporters at the United Nations, Marco Rubio reiterated, in so many words, that the Trump administration is seeking to replace the current Cuban leadership, and did not rule out the use of force to achieve that goal.
“The Cuban Revolution has failed. It has failed for sixty-something years, it’s a failure now,” Rubio said. “The question is what replaces it.”
He continued: “We’re open to measures moving forward that begin that process of change.”
Pressed on whether the Trump administration would try to repeat its tactics in Venezuela – where it raided the country in the dead of night, arrested former autocrat Nicolas Maduro, and ushered in a more US-friendly leader to replace him – Rubio equivocated, but did not rule out the possibility.
“If there is a threat to the national security of the United States, the president has both the power and the obligation to address it,” Rubio said. “That said, our preference always is to deal with these things – I don’t want to call it diplomatic – but in a negotiating way.”
He also said he believed that American business could play “a positive role in a future Cuba,” and that any new government would have to be friendlier to business interests. That comes in light of reporting by the Guardian

articles.title_orig: Taiwan, human rights are 'red lines' for China, ambassador says ahead of Trump, Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: Taiwan, human rights are 'red lines' for China, ambassador says ahead of Trump, Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Wife of American scholar wrongfully detained in China wants Trump to press Xi to release him
For over 100 days, Sylvia Zin has not been allowed to see or speak with her husband Min Zin, a U.S. citizen and scholar whose work focuses on Myanmar. She says he is being held without charge in China at a detention facility that is referred to by human rights groups as a "black site."
In an interview with CBS News, Sylvia Zin shared that the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS, has not formally charged him with a crime nor given him a trial date.
"They just said he's under investigation for endangering national security. That's all we know," she tearfully explained. "He's not a spy. He's not doing anything wrong."
She shared the terror of the first hours of Min's disappearance. His last message to her was a brief text on June 3 to tell her that he had landed in the Chinese city of Kunming. He had traveled there from his home in Thailand for an academic conference at the invitation of a Chinese professor. That night, Sylvia Zin received calls from Min Zin's worried colleagues.
"We started calling the immigration, the luggage — you know — carousel at the airport where he landed, the professor that invited him to see what happened to him," Sylvia Zin said. "He didn't check into the hotel, and so we knew, like, he was missing."
The next day, Sylvia Zin called the U.S. consulates in the area to ask for help. She then received a call from a +86 area code, indicating it was a Chinese phone number.
"I answered right away," she said, and described the caller's voice as "very heavily accented." She said she frantically took notes as the voice on the other end told her in English that the authorities were doing a "preliminary compulsory investigation."
"I didn't understand. I was trying to ask, like, 'What does that mean? Does it mean you have my husband?' You know, — what — 'how is he?' And then they just hung up," Sylvia said.
Held in undisclosed location without access to lawyer
Min Zin is being held by China's Ministry of State Security at a location classified as a "Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location" or RSDL, according to multiple sources closely tracking his case. Human rights groups refer to RSDLs as "black sites," since Chinese authorities take people into custody at undisclosed locations without providing them with access to a lawyer or judicial review. The United Nations considers RSDL use to be a form of enforced disappearance and possibly torture.
U.S. officials declined to comment on the conditions of Min Zin's captivity but confirmed to CBS News that Chinese authorities have permitted American consular officials to meet with him on a monthly basis in 30-minute increments at a nearby hotel.
Sylvia Zin described the three encounters that have so far taken place as heavily monitored. She has been told that her husband has lost weight and has developed knee pain, but Min Zin has not been permitted to discuss what has happened to him during his detention. He was able to say he was interrogated for four to six hours but she does not know how often he is being questioned.
She said that she has written letters to her husband for a U.S. official to read aloud to him. The family has retained an attorney, but Min Zin has not been permitted access to the lawyer.
"I want to know what I'm fighting against," Sylvia Zin told CBS News in the interview, which took place in Washington last Friday. "You know, do I prepare for a trial? If there's a purpose, you know, then I can kind of work towards that purpose, right?"
The State Department recently issued a warning to Americans traveling to mainland China due to "arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."
The warning states that Chinese law allows a wide range of information to be classified as state secrets. That could result in increased harassment of academics conducting research, businesspeople collecting data or journalists. Past work with the U.S. government may also make Americans a target.
Sylvia Zin and her husband both fled Burma, now known as Myanmar, in their youth during the pro-democracy movement in the 1980s. They became naturalized U.S. citizens and California residents. Min Zin runs a think tank, ISP-Myanmar, which studies China's role in Myanmar, which is run by a Beijing-backed military junta. U.S. officials confirmed that Min Zin's organization received U.S. government funding in the past, and this may have been a factor that drew Chinese scrutiny.
Sylvia Zin said she believes her husband was set up, since authorities arrested him shortly after his arrival in China. He had planned to attend an academic conference at a university with links to the Chinese state. Min Zin's June arrest appeared even more unusual given that he had been issued a 10-year multiple-entry visa and had visited Shanghai eight months earlier.
No detailed explanation for Min Zin's arrest from Chinese authorities
Multiple sources told CBS News that Chinese authorities have not provided a detailed explanation for Min Zin's arrest, and it remains unclear whether the MSS in Yunnan province conducted the arrest of its own volition or on the orders of the central government.
Sources indicated to CBS News that MSS authorities in that region typically oversee Beijing's interests in neighboring Myanmar, which may have been why Min Zin's work and his past advocacy for human rights were on their radar.
Doug Bandow, a senior foreign policy fellow at the CATO Institute, says Min Zin's work is likely the reason for his detention. "My bet would be that this is Chinese policy working as normal," Bandow told CBS News, "not a focus on the United States."
He thinks that China "wants to punish researchers who are revealing information they really don't want the world to know." Observing that Myanmar's military regime "has an awful international reputation," Bandow said China "would prefer not to be seen as a promoter of that regime.
"From their standpoint, this sends a message: Don't get too close to what we do in Myanmar," Bandow said.
Multiple sources told CBS News that the timing of Min Zin's June arrest was surprising, given that President Trump had just met weeks earlier with Chinese President Xi Jinping at a May summit and discussed others in Chinese captivity. Yet the very next month, Chinese authorities arbitrarily detained Min Zin.
"They want to test what…the United States' response would be. And if the response isn't very forceful, that shows that China can continue to do this and get away with it," said Josh Kurlantzick, an expert on Southeast Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations. He added that "it's a source of extra leverage" China may have in the summit Thursday between Xi and Mr. Trump.
Will Trump press Xi on Americans arbitrarily detained in China?
During a briefing with reporters ahead of the U.N. General Assembly, a Trump administration official was asked whether President Trump would raise the broad issue of Americans arbitrarily detained in China when he meets with Xi in Washington Thursday. The official said that Mr. Trump frequently "raises Americans that have been wrongfully detained and sometimes folks that aren't Americans that are wrongfully detained there in China."
The Trump administration did act in August, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio granted Min Zin the formal designation of having been "wrongfully detained." That legal designation pledges the full support of the U.S. government in seeking his release.
It followed what Assistant Secretary Dylan Johnson described as an extensive review of the circumstances of Min Zin's detention following his travel to a conference at the invitation of the Chinese government. In a statement, Johnson pledged that the U.S. would continue advocating for him and all U.S. citizens arbitrarily detained or exit banned from China.

articles.title_orig: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.title_zh: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.content_orig:
When the Milwaukee Bucks agreed to sign Gary Trent Jr. to a four-year, $64 million deal in July, red flags went up all around the league's office. Days later, reports emerged suggesting the NBA was looking into the signing , though details of the league's probe were scarce.
The league apparently found enough that it decided to launch a full-on investigation , according to The Athletic. The focus of that investigation: whether the Bucks used the contract as a way to circumvent the NBA salary cap.
The league reportedly hired law firm Hecker Fink to perform that investigation.
That particular accusation should sound familiar, as the league just wrapped an investigation on the Los Angeles Clippers and Kawhi Leonard that looked into the exact same thing. While both teams were accused of the same violation, their methods for allegedly circumventing the salary cap differ.
In the Clippers' case, the team was accused of using a team sponsor to funnel additional funds to Leonard as a way to get around NBA rules. Accusations surrounding the Bucks are far more straight forward.
The league is reportedly looking into whether the Bucks made handshake agreements with Trent to sign lesser deals the past two offseasons with the promise of Trent eventually receiving a much larger contract this offseason.
The issue stems from Trent's massive pay increase this offseason. After making $2.6 million with the Bucks in 2024 and $3.7 million in 2025, Trent's new deal will pay him an average of over $15 million the next four years.
That massive pay increase came after Trent experienced a down season, one in which he averaged just 8.1 points per game, his lowest scoring output since his rookie season.
When reached for comment by The Athletic, the NBA, Bucks and Trent's agency — Klutch Sports — all declined comment. Both the Bucks and Klutch are reportedly working with the NBA as it performs its investigation, per The Athletic.
Should the NBA determine the Bucks purposefully engaged in salary-cap circumvention, the team could see a similar punishment to the Clippers. The NBA came down hard on Los Angeles , docking the team five future first-round picks , fining and suspending team owner Steve Ballmer and fining Leonard.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's (MCD) has one final shot this year to supersize its stock price.
And that Hail Mary toss will happen in Chicago on Wednesday at a closely watched investor day.
"We think the Sep 23 Investor Day could prove a crucial clearing event in which management articulates a credible path to reaccelerating same-store sales in the 4Q/2027, protecting & growing operating margins (w/ potential SG&A leverage starting next year), and still accelerating unit growth despite the tough macro," Jefferies analyst Andy Barish wrote. "For the stock to rebound, management will have to convince investors the recent same-store sales slowdown is fixable (soon) and restore confidence in the long-term growth algo."
It has been a dreadful year for the Golden Arches — one punctuated by an 18% drop in the stock price.
Comparable sales for a resurgent Restaurant Brands International-owned (QSR) Burger King US rose 8.5% year over year, beating analyst expectations, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. The result trounced McDonald's US result, which reported a disappointing 0.8% comparable sales gain.
McDonald's entered the fall with a black eye, given the barrage of key initiatives it recently launched and plans to launch.
First, McDonald's debuted its new McValue menu by offering 10 items under $3.
It then launched six new drinks on May 6, with refreshers like Strawberry Watermelon and crafted sodas like Sprite Berry Blast. All the drinks are caffeinated and aimed at Gen Z consumers who have been going to the nearest Dutch Bros (BROS) or convenience store for a Celsius (CELH).
A nationwide Aug. 17 rollout of its Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer ensued.
But the revamped McValue platform, discounted breakfast offers, and broader push into specialty beverages all failed to generate the incremental traffic McDonald's was banking on in the second quarter.
Investors are hoping to hear a different tune tomorrow.
"While lower-income consumer trends and highly promotional QSR environment don't provide much support, we view strategic missteps as largely responsible for the recent slowdown in same-store sales/traffic, much or all of which can be addressed in the 4Q and '27 to reaccelerate trends," Barish wrote.
"We expect a relatively quick adjustment to the marketing and menu innovation calendars that drove execution issues in the summer as management and franchisees return to a workable balance (some digital promos returned Aug 10, Spicy Chicken McNuggets limited-time offer came back Sept. 1, Spongebob x One Piece promo starts 9/15)," Barish added. "Work around franchisee pricing and participation in promos and value offerings could take longer, we expect an update on convos w/ franchisees next week. Finally, growing awareness of the new premium bevs (Red Bull launched Aug 17), Rewards, digital/delivery, and EDAP provides at least a steady floor."

articles.title_orig: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.title_zh: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.content_orig:
FIRST ON FOX: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping about the future of artificial intelligence, two top House Republicans are warning that the Chinese Communist Party is "throwing gasoline on the fire" by undermining America's effort to build out AI infrastructure.
In a new letter disclosed to Fox News Digital, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., and House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano to determine whether money has been funneled from overseas through America’s charitable system to block the data centers needed for the U.S. to compete with China.
Specifically, they raised questions about hundreds of millions of dollars that American-born communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham pumped into nonprofits and organizations that are now among the leading organizations fighting data center development throughout the country. Recipients of Singham's largesse include the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, both self-described pro-China communist groups. Earlier this month, activists from both groups carried signs in a Chapel Hill, N.C., protest, merging anti-Trump sentiments with support for communist Cuba and opposition to data centers and AI development, including the message, "SHUT IT DOWN!"
"Under no circumstances can we allow an adversary, and our most serious competitor in AI infrastructure, to weaponize our own tax code and harm an emerging American industry," the lawmakers wrote in the letter, sent on Tuesday.
FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP
The lawmakers allege that influence operations linked to China are exploiting tax-exempt organizations, nonprofit networks and social media campaigns to fuel opposition to the data centers needed to power America’s AI industry.
The lawmakers urged the agencies to investigate whether tax-exempt organizations connected to the network have operated for the "private or political benefit of foreign-aligned interests" and whether donor-advised funds and intermediary entities were used to "launder the origin of foreign-directed money into American advocacy."
A Fox News Digital investigation found that Singham funneled $285 million since 2017 to six U.S. nonprofits, including his wife Jodie Evans' group, CodePink, through two shell corporations and a donor-advised philanthropy fund run by Goldman Sachs, which said it closed the Singham account in 2024.
The nonprofits have functioned with tax-deductible status while actively involved in promoting communist regimes such as China, coordinating street protests and fomenting anti-American rage. They have denied being part of any foreign influence operation, and Singham hasn't responded to requests for comment.
Smith said China is helping fuel opposition to American artificial intelligence infrastructure by giving a base to Singham as he funds U.S. nonprofit groups involved in anti-data-center protests.
"This is the Chinese helping throw the gasoline on the fire," Smith told Fox News Digital. "The American people need to know that this is not just an organic movement."
Smith said Americans have legitimate concerns about data centers, including their effect on electricity costs and water usage. But he said foreign-backed organizations shouldn't be allowed to exploit those concerns to slow U.S. technological development.
Smith said that "the Chinese want to stall and slow down the advancement of AI in the United States because they want to win the AI war."
"Tax exempt is a privilege. It is not a right," Smith said. "We need to make sure that we’re not subsidizing tax dollars to help create hostility and unrest in our country."
Smith also called for greater transparency regarding the flow of money among organizations connected to Singham. He added that the broader issue extends beyond the tax code and could include questions about compliance with the Foreign Agents Registration Act violations. "Transparency is the biggest thing," he said.
PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS
Moolenaar said organizations presenting themselves as grassroots opposition groups are actually advancing the Chinese Communist Party’s agenda in the U.S. "Groups that portray themselves as grassroots are really more AstroTurf — very fake — being funded by entities that are working in partnership with the Chinese Communist Party," Moolenaar told Fox News Digital.
"The concern is that they are manipulating the messaging and opposition to different American investments, whether it’s data centers or other technological advances, trying to turn the American people against these technologies so that China would be able to have dominance in this area," he said.
Moolenaar pointed to the use of grassroots organizations, community groups, propaganda and online bots.
"We don’t want foreign entities of concern — countries that may be opposed to American interests — using our system against the American people and trying to manipulate them," Moolenaar said.
He said the lawmakers are seeking greater transparency into the organizations’ funding and tax-exempt status, including whether their political activity violates federal rules.
"When you see them actively speaking out against American interests and realize that groups like CodePink are aggressively funded by this network, that raises serious concerns," Moolenaar said.
The chairman said China’s influence efforts exploit the openness of American society.
"The Chinese Communist Party always has the goal of dividing Americans, manipulating and getting their propaganda out," he said. "They don’t have the freedoms that we enjoy, and they try to exploit our freedoms and use that against us."
China remains both a major trading partner and a strategic competitor, Moolenaar said, but the United States must avoid becoming dependent on Beijing.
"They are a serious adversary," he said. "They are a trading partner, which is true, and we need to have a relationship with them," Moolenaar said. "But at the same time, we do not want to be manipulated, we do not want to become more dependent, and we certainly do not want to be under their thumb."
The lawmakers noted that a bicameral group of congressional committees, including the Ways and Means Committee, the House Select Committee on the CCP and the Senate Intelligence Committee, has been examining how influence operations linked to the CCP allegedly exploit America’s tax-exempt sector to "sow discord and undermine our democracy."
"The CCP consistently identifies political issues under public debate in our country and seeks to corrupt those debates," Smith and Moolenaar wrote in their letter. The CCP, they added, seeks to "heighten divisions between Americans and to degrade our civic processes."
The lawmakers specifically pointed to opposition campaigns targeting the construction of data centers, which are critical to the nation’s AI infrastructure.
A June report from OpenAI identified two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating in China that were used in covert influence operations targeting U.S. debates over AI and technology policy. One campaign, dubbed "Data Center Bandwagon," generated social media comments and images claiming that data-center construction was raising electricity prices for average families. OpenAI said it found no evidence that the operation achieved meaningful breakout beyond its own activity, but said it demonstrated how foreign operators can exploit existing local concerns to amplify distrust.

articles.title_orig: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Garoppolo and 4 other names for NFL teams in need of a quarterback
articles.title_zh: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Garoppolo and 4 other names for NFL teams in need of a quarterback
articles.content_orig:
The NFL season is only two weeks old, and yet six teams have already dealt with injuries to their starting quarterbacks.
The Falcons were already without Michael Penix Jr. because of his recovery from an ACL injury when Tua Tagovailoa went down with a back injury just days before the opener. In Week 1, the Seahawks lost Sam Darnold to a glute injury and Vikings starter Kyler Murray suffered a concussion. Week 2 was even worse: The Commanders lost Jayden Daniels to another dislocated elbow (the same one he dislocated last season), the Bears watched Caleb Williams get carted off with a hamstring injury and then placed backup Tyler Bagent in the concussion protocol , and the Giants saw Jaxson Dart go down with a knee injury whose severity is still to be determined.
The spate of early injuries to quarterbacks has reinforced the value of experienced (and reliable) backups. The teams that have them have remained competitive; Seattle and Minnesota are both 2-0 with respective backups Drew Lock and Carson Wentz filling in.
But the teams that lack a solid No. 2 or any real depth at the position have paid a price. Just look at Atlanta, where third-stringer Cooper Rush was benched during a blowout loss to the Panthers after throwing his fourth pick of the season. He was replaced by Jack Strand -- who promptly threw a pick-six.
There's good news in store for a few teams. Penix will start for the Falcons on Thursday night and Tagovailoa is back to fully participating in practice. Darnold is expected to return to practice in some capacity this week for the Seahawks and Murray has been cleared from the concussion protocol in Minnesota.
But that leaves three teams who could potentially be in search of reinforcement.
Case Keenum is the only other quarterback on the Bears' active roster and, although he has 66 starts in his 14-year NFL career, he hasn't played a regular-season snap since December 2023.
In Washington, it remains unclear how much time Daniels might miss. X-rays of Daniels' elbow were negative for any fractures, but coach Dan Quinn declined to provide any details about the MRI results. Daniels will not start Sunday against the Seahawks, but how long he'll be out thereafter is unknown. In the meantime, the Commanders will turn to Marcus Mariota , just as they have the last two seasons when Daniels has dealt with injuries. The difference this time around: Washington doesn't have an experienced third-string QB like they did in Josh Johnson last year. The team's current No. 3 is seventh-round rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, a young player who showed some promise in preseason but is still quite green.
The Giants are in a similar if not worse position. Dart could be out for the rest of the season, a much worse outcome than what was originally expected. Jameis Winston is expected to take over as the starter, but he's the only other quarterback on the Giants' active roster. Jake Haener, a fourth-round pick by the Saints in 2023, is on the practice squad.
So who might be available to help?
Finding a quality backup quarterback at this point in the season is difficult, but there are a number of veterans and young QBs who could serve as extra insurance, if not more, for teams in need. From potential trade candidates to street free agents and practice squad players, here are some players who may be under consideration, either now or after the next prominent starter goes down.
The sixth-year quarterback has seemingly found his groove in San Francisco as Brock Purdy's backup. After a standout rookie season with the Patriots in which he was named a Pro Bowl alternate, Jones cycled through multiple play callers and quickly regressed. He was traded to Jacksonville in 2024 and started seven of 10 games in relief of Trevor Lawrence. But it wasn't until he signed a two-year deal with the 49ers in 2025 that he really showed his worth as a reliable backup. He went 5-3 as a fill-in starter, recording a 69.6 completion percentage, averaging 7.4 yards per attempt and compiling a 97.4 passer rating -- all career bests. San Fran may want to hold onto him to spell Purdy, but it could also get a decent return from a desperate team for a player who is set to be a free agent after this season.
The 12-year veteran and two-time Super Bowl winner reportedly considered retirement in the offseason, but ultimately decided to keep his options open in the NFL. Garoppolo, 34,  hasn't had any real playing time since the 2024 season, when he started the Rams' regular-season finale against the Seahawks, and he hasn't had any consistent playing time since the start of the 2023 season, with the Raiders. But he does have a 43-21 record as a starter, to go with a 67.4 career completion percentage and 97.7 passer rating.
Johnson, 40, is in his 19th season of professional football and still going, as a member of the Bengals' practice squad. He is the ultimate journeyman, playing for a record 14 NFL teams. Johnson was Washington's third-string quarterback last season until Daniels went down and he became the backup and then the starter late in the season when Mariota suffered a quad injury. His familiarity with offensive coordinator David Blough and Washington's other quarterbacks could make him a viable option if the Commanders seek outside reinforcement. But Johnson also has deep ties to Giants coach John Harbaugh (and his brother). Johnson had three stints with the Ravens when Harbaugh was their head coach, totaling seven games (one start) and completing 69.8 percent of his passes for 321 passing yards, two TDs, a pick and a 97.1 passer rating.
Levis signed to the Jets' practice squad on Tuesday, so should the Giants be interested in adding him to their active roster, he'd have a pretty easy move. But would they? The 2023 second-round pick by the Titans showed some promise when he took over for Ryan Tannehill as a rookie in 2023. But injuries and poor performances derailed his tenure in Tennessee. He was benched late in the 2024 season, when Giants quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan was Tennessee's head coach. Levis missed all of 2025 because of a shoulder injury and was released last month after losing the backup job to Mitchell Trubisky.
Richardson never developed into the franchise quarterback the Colts hoped he'd be when they drafted him fourth overall in 2023. Injuries, performance issues and general readiness questions after he tapped out for a play during a narrow loss to the Texans in '24 put him on the outs with the organization. He lost his starting job to Daniel Jones, requested a trade and is now in the final year of his rookie contract (the Colts declined his fifth-year option). If Richardson is viewed as more of a developmental project, then a team in need of immediate help may be unlikely to trade for him. But never say never.
The same context holds for McCarthy, the Vikings' 2024 first-round pick. McCarthy missed the entirety of his rookie season because of a torn meniscus and was sidelined for seven games last season because of injuries. McCarthy fell to third string this season after the team signed Murray to start and re-signed Wentz as his backup. McCarthy has started only 10 games and has more interceptions (12) than touchdowns (11). But he's well-liked in the Harbaugh family. John Harbaugh's brother, Jim, once lauded McCarthy as the greatest quarterback in Michigan history.
The 10-year veteran has spent more than four seasons with Callahan: three in Cincinnati, when Callahan was the Bengals' coordinator; another in Tennessee, when Callahan was head coach, and this offseason with the Giants. Allen was among the roster cuts late last month.
This article originally appeared in The Athletic .

articles.title_orig: Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China
articles.title_zh: Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has spent years trying to squeeze China — imposing tariffs, cutting off access to advanced technology and pressing U.S. allies to reduce their dependence on Beijing. When he begins meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, he'll juxtapose the longstanding bluster with the pomp and circumstance the leaders lavish on each other.
And the two-day tête-à-tête will take place as Trump confronts a China that has proved harder to isolate and allies increasingly reluctant to line up behind the U.S. to do it.
Part of that is Beijing's doing. China has deepened trade ties around the world while building leverage of its own, most notably through rare earths. Its global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year, reaching a record $1.2 trillion for 2025 even as its exports to the U.S. dropped.
But the shift also reflects Trump's approach. Since returning to office, fights over tariffs, defense spending and personal spats have strained relationships with traditional allies even as Trump has pursued a more transactional relationship with Xi.
Countries Washington has traditionally counted on to magnify its power are increasingly seeking room to maneuver between the world's two largest economies.
As a result, Trump enters Thursday's summit facing a test of whether strains with U.S. allies have made it harder to marshal American power against Xi.
"China is presenting itself to the world as the stable counterweight to an erratic and violent United States," said Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution think tank. "America retains unmatched power on the world stage, but leverage requires a united front and there are a shrinking number of countries willing to follow America's lead right now."
For decades, one of the U.S.'s biggest advantages over China has been its network of allies and partners. When the U.S. restricted technology or imposed sanctions, bringing major economies in Europe and Asia along made those measures harder for Beijing to evade.
China still lacks anything comparable: The Lowy Institute, an independent Australian foreign-policy think tank, scored the U.S. defense networks at 81.4 on a scale of 100, versus 18.9 for China in 2025. But Beijing does not need U.S. allies to switch sides to erode that advantage. It only needs them to become less willing to move with Washington, Hass and other China experts said.
"When democratic countries don't have public support for a counterpart, it raises the cost for leaders to align with the United States," Hass told CNBC. "It lowers the cost for leaders to defy the United States."
Trump has taken sledgehammer to relationships with allies. He's clashed with NATO over defense spending, threatened to reduce the U.S. troop presence in much of Europe while announcing plans Tuesday to add troops in Greenland after threatening to take over the island and imposed tariffs on the U.S.'s northern neighbor Canada.
"Although our biggest economic complaints regarding China's economy are shared by many of our allies and partners, the current U.S. approach is to attack all of those countries ... instead of forming a common front," said Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
Meanwhile, public confidence in the U.S. as a reliable partner has fallen. In Canada, the share of people who described the U.S. as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% this year, according to Pew Research Center in June. In Germany, the share who said Washington considers other countries' interests when making foreign policy fell from 60% in 2023 to 23%.
Canada this month was invited to be the first "associate member" of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government seeks deeper defense ties with Europe and less reliance on the U.S.
Foreign allies "worry that as soon as they make a deal with us, Washington will undercut them in some way that they will then regret," Hart told CNBC.
China has sought to capitalize on that opening, not necessarily by persuading countries to choose Beijing over Washington, but by making the choice less binary.
The country remains a U.S. security partner and a strategic competitor of China, with troops from both countries still deployed along their disputed Himalayan border. Yet Xi visited India this month for the first time in seven years as the two countries took what Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings, called "baby steps" toward stabilizing relations.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese data, and Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to strengthen business and transport links despite unresolved security disputes.
"Uncertainty over Trump's approach to Beijing and strains in India's own relationship with the U.S. have given India another reason to keep relations with China on steadier ground," Madan told CNBC. "Even a tactical détente between the U.S. India and China can have downstream impacts on India's strategic environment.
The changing balance of leverage is most tangible in the economic relationship.
Trump's tariffs targeted China's reliance on U.S. buyers, while U.S. export controls targeted a deeper dependency: the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment Beijing needs to compete at the technological frontier.
Those pressure points remain. But Beijing has developed leverage of its own. China placed seven rare-earth elements under export controls last year, forcing companies to seek government approval to ship them abroad. China controls roughly 70% of global rare-earth mining and more than 87% of refining and production in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
In short order, Ford halted Explorer production in Chicago for a week amid magnet shortages, while Japanese and European auto suppliers shut production lines awaiting materials.
Suddenly, the U.S. faced a version of the vulnerability it had spent years trying to create for Beijing: dependence on something the other side could withhold.
"One of China's primary objectives ahead of these meetings is to box the U.S. in diplomatically, to limit the Trump administration's range of action," Hart said, pointing to critical minerals as one tool Beijing has used.
That vulnerability now hangs over Thursday's summit. The current trade truce expires Nov. 10. Rare earths were again on the table in weekend talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
But Trump still has cards to play.
U.S. and allied firms control critical parts of the advanced semiconductor ecosystem, and American restrictions limit China's access to its most sophisticated chips and manufacturing equipment. Trump has also allowed limited sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China even as broader restrictions remain in place, making semiconductor access another bargaining point.
That bargaining dynamic is beginning to reach beyond trade.
A $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and called it a "very good negotiating chip."
For Beijing, few issues carry higher stakes. China claims Taiwan as its sovereign territory and has never renounced the use of force to achieve unification. Xi also pressed Trump on U.S. arms sales and Taiwan during their May meeting.
The delayed arms deal has raised concern among U.S. allies in Asia that Trump could soften Washington's position on Taiwan in exchange for economic concessions from Xi.
But Hart said Beijing's objective goes beyond one arms package.
"Their bigger play will be getting him to feel like he has a deal with Xi Jinping underway" in which Trump believes he needs to hold back U.S. support for Taiwan, Hart said. "They clearly have gained ground there when it comes to the $14 billion arms deal."

articles.title_orig: As the US and China race on AI, the Vatican presses for global safeguards
articles.title_zh: As the US and China race on AI, the Vatican presses for global safeguards
articles.content_orig:
As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to agree to only limited cooperation on AI safety at summit.
As industry leaders urge a global slowdown in artificial intelligence development for the sake of humanity, the two superpowers driving the technology’s rapid advancement have given no indication they intend to hit the brakes.
The United States and China, which are locked in a fierce strategic rivalry, have each rebutted calls to slow the pace of AI development, even as industry executives and researchers stress the need for international cooperation to avoid exposing humans to catastrophic – or even existential – risks.

As US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet on Wednesday in Washington, DC, for the third time this year, expectations for cooperation on AI safety are modest. Observers anticipated measures that, at best, would fall far short of the coordinated slowdown that many experts said is needed.
“The two countries host nearly all frontier labs and most of the models people download,” said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, describing agreed guardrails between the US and China as “close to a precondition” for safe AI.
“A safety regime covering one side’s models covers half the problem,” Wang Graylin said.
Hampering the prospects for US-China cooperation, analysts said, are mutual mistrust and divergent perceptions of the primary risks involved.
Trump has dismissed fears about AI as a “conspiracy” and suggested guardrails are not needed under his leadership, stressing the need for the US to stay ahead of China in the frontier technology.
Trump, who has cast AI dominance as crucial to the US maintaining its position as the top global power, on Tuesday again poured cold water on hopes for international cooperation, telling the United Nations General Assembly that Washington would oppose any “globalist scheme” to control AI.
China has taken a more hands-on approach to AI regulation – releasing the third iteration of its security framework this month – but has similarly rebuffed calls for a slowdown, dismissing fears of existential risks aired in Silicon Valley as “fearmongering”.
While Chinese officials have raised concerns about the dangers of AI, they have related it to more prosaic concerns, including cybersecurity and the authority of the ruling Communist Party.
In a rare essay this month, Chinese Minister of State Security Chen Yixin warned of “hostile forces” using AI to “fabricate political rumours” and “incite antagonistic sentiments”, threatening “political security, institutional security and ideological security”.
“China also increasingly recognises loss of control, misuse and cyber-risks but is much more sensitive to the possibility that ‘AI safety’ could become a justification for restricting Chinese access to chips, computers or markets,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“So the deepest obstacle is whether both sides can separate genuine safety cooperation from the wider technology competition,” Sun said.
“If every safety discussion is linked to export controls or slowing China’s development, Beijing will naturally question the purpose of cooperation,” Sun added.
So far, the only proposals publicly floated by either side have been a US-China dialogue and a notification mechanism for reporting national security threats.
While those measures would be positive first steps, the US and China would still need to reach an agreement on the AI capabilities or uses that should be off-limits to avert the greatest threats, experts said.
There is no consensus within the AI sector about how the technology should be regulated – or even whether government-led supervision is needed at all.
While AI leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have called for a slowdown and greater regulation, some experts argued that such calls do not go far enough and development should be paused outright.
“International coordination is absolutely critical. We need more than safeguards,” said David Krueger, an assistant professor at the University of Montreal who specialises in AI safety.
“We need an immediate, indefinite international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
Other key figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, have played down the need for external oversight and emphasised AI’s potential to deliver transformative benefits for society.
Among those most alarmed at the rapid pace of AI development, recursive self-improvement, which describes when AI models learn to improve themselves, is often identified as a critical tipping point.
In an essay this month urging the AI sector to “pace the frontier”, Amodei said the US and China should discuss an agreement to “substantially limit” the rate of AI development while acknowledging that any deal is unlikely given the potential for a rule-breaking party to shift the global balance of power.
“The US and China must agree on AI capabilities red lines that will not be crossed. Most crucially, AI must never get powerful enough for recursive self-improvement,” said Otto Barten, director of the Netherlands-based Existential Risk Observatory.
“We do not know where the positive feedback loop of ever-smarter AIs creating ever-smarter AIs without human supervision will end and what these agents will finally be able to do,” Barten added.
Wang Graylin said Washington and Beijing should come to an agreement on what constitutes an “unacceptable capability” and a common standard to test frontier models, ideally by an independent international body that is funded by multiple countries.
But Wang Graylin acknowledged that distrust is clouding the prospects for an agreement and US officials are likely to see any deal as impossible to verify.
“Verification is hard for software you cannot see,” he said.
Sun said the US could ease the path to cooperation by “drawing a clearer line” between policies aimed at AI safety and those intended to maintain Washington’s technological advantage.
China could also contribute to greater trust by providing “greater transparency about its safety practices, model-evaluation methods and incident-reporting mechanisms,” Sun said.
Henry Gao, an expert on China and trade law at Singapore Management University, said a deeper issue is a fundamental mismatch in how Washington and Beijing view AI risks.
“Many in the US AI-safety debate focus on the possibility of highly capable AI escaping human control and posing catastrophic risks to humanity,” Gao said.
“In China, national security concerns appear more geopolitical: A major perceived danger is that the US could gain a decisive AI advantage and use it against China,” Gao said.
“That creates pressure to accelerate rather than slow development.”
Some AI experts argued that the focus of a US-China dialogue should be on mitigating existing risks rather than slowing development outright.
“AI is already extremely useful and has the potential to improve lives around the world,” said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and the founder of the Tech Buzz China news site, adding that pausing development would also impact the technology’s positive applications.
“I think thoughtful rules of engagement, constant monitoring, open channels of communication and the ability to adjust our approach as AI acquires different capabilities are much more important,” Ma said.
“The safeguards need to evolve alongside the technology.”

articles.title_orig: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Quarterback injuries have been the unfortunate story of the 2026 NFL season thus far. The loss of six starters from training camp through Week 2 overshadows on-field play for nearly one quarter of the league. Fortunately, many of the injuries are short-term issues with only a slight risk of derailing the campaign, but in a couple of cases, there is little reason for optimism.
The New York Giants might be in the worst position of any of the six teams that lost their starters. Jaxson Dart sustained a knee injury on "Monday Night Football" that, upon further testing, is more severe than the team initially feared. If any of the NFL's injured signal-callers are to miss the rest of the year, Dart is the most likely candidate.
If it is indeed a season-ender for Dart, the Giants' 2026 goals shift dramatically. For other teams, like the Seattle Seahawks, expectations remain largely unchanged even in the face of injury.
Here are reasonable expectations for all six teams with injured quarterbacks.
Injured player: Jaxson Dart (knee)
New expectations: Vie for another early draft pick
There is no sugar coating the Giants' outlook without Dart. What had all the makings of a (finally) exciting year is already down the tubes. The offense looked hapless with Jameis Winston on in relief against the Los Angeles Rams, and while the veteran has had decent stretches in the past, his diminished arm strength, persistent turnover problems and the immense downgrade in mobility he brings compared to Dart puts a firm ceiling on the Giants.
Winston will potentially man the offense for the remainder of the year after Dart's MRI revealed a worse injury than expected. In five games without Dart since his arrival as a first-round pick, the Giants are 0-5. That history suggests that so long as Winston is the man under center, New York will stand among the worst teams in the NFL. The silver lining is that the Giants should be able to add more premium young talent to their enticing core in the 2027 draft, but this was supposed to be a season in which that group elevated them out of the early draft pick range and into playoff contention.
Injured players: Caleb Williams (hamstring), Tyson Bagent (concussion)
New expectations: Fall into early-season hole, climb out when Williams returns
The hamstring issue that knocked Williams out of the Week 2 loss to the Minnesota Vikings initially looked like it would result in a long-term absence. Instead, the rising star is week-to-week and could even return as soon as Monday's battle with the Philadelphia Eagles. It would be aggressive to bring him back from a soft-tissue injury in such short order, though, and with Bagent suffering a concussion, there is a real chance the Bears roll out their No. 3 quarterback on "Monday Night Football." Case Keenum might make his first appearance since 2023.
If it ends up being no more than a one-game absence for Williams, the Bears will likely be 1-2 upon his return. The early-season losses might hold Chicago back from reaching its loftiest regular-season goals, but by no means would they dash the Bears' hopes of reaching the playoffs. The offense is electric enough with Williams in the lineup to rattle off a bunch of victories. Remember, this team started 0-2 a year ago and reached the divisional round of the playoffs.
Injured player: Jayden Daniels (dislocated elbow)
New expectations: Another losing season incoming
With two losses already on their ledger, the Commanders are in extreme danger of falling back into the NFL's bottom tier for a second consecutive season. It is difficult to foresee them stringing together wins with Daniels on the sideline, particularly because their next six games include matchups against the NFC West's top three teams and a rematch with the Eagles squad that defeated them in Week 1. Washington might have to attack that entire stretch with Marcus Mariota under center.
The dislocated elbow is the exact same injury Daniels sustained in Week 9 last year. He missed four weeks and reinjured the elbow in his return and sat out the remainder of the season. The recurring nature of this issue sounds alarms about Daniels' ability to stay on the field this year and beyond. And the rest of the team is not strong enough to stay afloat without him. The defense, for instance, ranks 27th in scoring through two games.
Injured player: Sam Darnold (glute)
New expectations: Contend for second consecutive Super Bowl
Drew Lock did just enough to lead the Seahawks to a season-opening win when thrust into action in the first quarter, and following a full week of preparation for the road opener at the Arizona Cardinals, he excelled with three touchdowns in a 31-7 win. Seattle should be in business for as long as it needs to roll out its backup.
Even better news for the Seahawks is that Sam Darnold might return to action this week. Coach Mike Macdonald said he anticipates Darnold suiting up for practice, and the extent of his participation will determine his availability for Sunday's matchup against the Commanders. Assuming the offense is back at full strength no later than Week 4, the Seahawks have a good chance of remaining undefeated in time for Darnold's return. They cannot ask for much more than that.
Injured player: Kyler Murray (concussion)
New expectations: Battle for NFC North title
The concussion Murray suffered in the first quarter of the season opener looked grim, but it will result in only a one-game absence. Murray cleared concussion protocol and will start in Week 3 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, coach Kevin O'Connell announced. Thanks to Carson Wentz and two solid performances, Murray inherits a 2-0 record for his return.
In a division where every other team is 1-1 and where the Bears have quarterback injuries, the Packers look flawed, and the Lions' defense is a mess, Minnesota has a chance to build a comfortable early-season cushion. None of the teams on their schedule until Week 9 made the playoffs in 2025. If Murray delivers the career resurgence the Vikings hoped he would when they signed him in free agency, he could lead them to a terrific first half of the season.
Injured player: Michael Penix Jr. (torn ACL), Tua Tagovailoa (oblique)
New expectations: Prevent disastrous season after 0-2 start
The Cooper Rush experience was dismal. Back-to-back losses and a 34-3 drubbing at the hands of a division rival made the Falcons look like one of the NFL's worst teams through two weeks. Help is on the way, though. Penix is cleared for action and will take over as the starter in Week 3, and Tagovailoa returned to full participation in practice, setting him up to assume backup duties. Health willing, Atlanta will not need to turn back to its No. 3 quarterback.
The problem is that Penix is not guaranteed to be an upgrade. He is 4-8 as a starter since his arrival in 2024 and has an immense injury history. He ought to be able to make better use of his elite offensive supporting cast than Rush, but it would require a breakout season from the third-year pro in order for the Falcons to erase their 0-2 start and finish the year above .500. And if things go sideways for Penix or he returns to the injury report, Tagovailoa carries the exact same shortcomings.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
The S&P 500 dropped 0.6%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 313 points, or 0.6%.
Declines in utilities, consumer discretionary and communication services stocks led the broader market's fall, with the three sectors shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot . The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.087%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since June 2024 at 4.887%.
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 73% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
Crude oil futures moved up as well. Brent crude futures for November delivery were last seen trading 3% higher at around $102 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 2% at around $92 per barrel.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, though the index is about 0.8% off from its all-time high.
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.
Selig also told CNBC the federal regulator has a zero tolerance policy on wash trading, after growing concerns that Kalshi has wash trading on its perpetual futures trades. The Wall Street Journal reported the CFTC is looking into the trades.
The chairman also touched on Kalshi's efforts to introduce margin trading to traders. Selig said the CFTC is evaluating the proposal and that it will allow only traders meeting "stringent eligibility criteria" to participate.
Treasury yields raced higher on Wednesday as new services and manufacturing sector data increased worry of further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The 2-year Treasury note yield jumped 8 basis points to 4.464%. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield popped 7 basis points to 5.058%, a level not seen since July 2007. The 30-year Treasury yield gained more than 4 basis points to 5.347%.
Read the full story here .
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday he expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further to tame inflation.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way. Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded," he said in remarks for a housing conference in Chicago.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he added. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Barr labeled last week's quarter percentage point rate hike "important action" for policy that was "out of position" in getting inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.
The remarks came as S&P Global reported that its flash readings on services and manufacturing hit their highest levels since 2021. Price pressures are also surged, posting their highest readings since October 2022.
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.
The S&P 500 lost 0.1% just after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 156 points, or 0.3%.

articles.title_orig: US Air Force to shut down research centre focusing on Chinese military
articles.title_zh: US Air Force to shut down research centre focusing on Chinese military
articles.content_orig:
US Air Force to shut down research centre focusing on Chinese military
The China Aerospace Studies Institute published open-source research on the PLA’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities
The US Air Force is shutting down a major research centre dedicated to open-source analysis of the Chinese military’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities.
The China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) said in a statement on Tuesday that Air University, the US Air Force institution under which it operates, had decided to close the institute, with all of its roles becoming unfunded from October 1.
CASI said its employees would continue to work and get paid for now and that it expected to honour its existing commitments “through at least March of 2027”.
The institute will continue publishing articles and reports already in the pipeline and conducting courses on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that it has already committed to provide to air force units. However, a 10th anniversary event scheduled for February will be cancelled.

articles.title_orig: Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump
articles.title_zh: Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump
articles.content_orig: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-lead-in-new-poll-as-trump-looms-over-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump Politics Updated on Sep 23, 2026 9:34 AM EDT — Published on Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT President Donald Trump's efforts to make the midterm elections a referendum on his presidency appear to be backfiring as Democratic congressional candidates hold a significant lead over Republicans in the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Independents, who often decide competitive races, favor Democrats by a margin of 25 points. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Driving this sentiment is a president who isn't on the ballot but has asked voters to pretend he is. About 7 in 10 voters acknowledge the president is a factor, one way or another, in their vote for Congress. Just 30% of voters say Trump isn't a factor in their vote. "The Democrats are sitting in a very good place," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. "There's a lot of grumbling in the electorate and a lot of sentiment for changing things around." More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Graphic by Steff Staples/PBS News. Trump bragged of Republicans riding his electoral coattails during his speech to the party's midterm convention in Dallas this month, building his strategy on the premise that voters turn out for him and not for anyone else. His appeal is effective largely among self-identified MAGA supporters; 71% say in this poll that their vote for Congress is mostly a vote for the president. But with absentee and mail voting already underway in a handful of states, the poll suggests Trump's influence may have the opposite effect on other voters. Overall, 45% of registered voters and 54% of independents say their vote will be mostly to express their opposition to Trump. Eight in 10 Democrats are motivated to vote against Trump. Just 24% of voters and 12% of independents say they are voting to show support for the president. "That's devastating," Democratic strategist Joel Payne said. In this political environment, he added, it's expected that political partisans will line up behind their team, but when independents are strongly motivated to vote against one side, "that's significant." The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in this latest poll. But that top line understates the asymmetry: More than half of voters – 53% – strongly disapprove of the job he's doing, the highest share recorded by Marist across either of his terms in office, and on par with high voter dissatisfaction with Trump in the aftermath of the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Congressional Republicans have little room to run from Trump. "It's a nationalized election whether they like it or not," Miringoff said. The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. Graphic by Dan Cooney/PBS News. Thirteen incumbents were defeated in their primaries this year, and dozens of members announced plans to retire or run for another office. Nearly one in five lawmakers who started this Congress will not return for the next one, according to an NPR analysis, driven by record-setting retirements and primary defeats. READ MORE: Rising gas prices frustrate voters. Trump says it's an 'inexpensive price to pay' for the Iran war With gas prices, the war in Iran and other national issues dominating, he said, "it'd be next to impossible" for a congressional candidate to ignore those and focus only on local issues. "It's not believable enough because [Trump's] such a dominant force." "These numbers are concerning to Republicans behind the scenes," Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. Abdul wondered whether the president's luck had run out. "It's almost like he's Icarus," the famous figure from Greek mythology, he said. The question is whether Trump's "gotten a bit too close to the sun this time." Republicans lag in enthusiasm The premise behind Trump's plea to pretend he's on the ballot points to a potential turnout problem among his base. The poll shows few signs that his appeal is closing the enthusiasm gap. Voters overall are highly engaged. Nearly 9 in 10 say they care a great deal or quite a bit about which party controls Congress, and 75% say they're following the midterm elections closely. But the passion tilts toward Democrats. Seventy-six percent of Democrats say they care a great deal who wins Congress, while 67% of Republicans say the same. Additionally, 42% of Democrats are following the election very closely compared to 34% of Republicans. Trump's most loyal supporters match Democrats' fervor. Three-quarters of MAGA supporters care a great deal about the outcome. But the rest of the Republican coalition that Trump is asking to show up is lagging behind. Independents are the least engaged of all, with 30% following the race very closely. Miringoff said that gap is the problem Trump's messaging is trying to solve. "When he's not on the ballot, it doesn't automatically transfer," he said. The calculation Republicans have had to make, he added, is that "the enthusiasm factor for their base is a little soft." History is often unkind to a president in Trump's position File photo: President Donald Trump arrives on stage Sept. 9 at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas. Photo by Evan Vucci/Reuters/File Photo In the last 90 years, the incumbent president's party has lost an average of 27 seats in the House of Representatives and three seats in the Senate in midterm elections, according to a recent UC Santa Barbara analysis. In the 2018 midterm elections during Trump's first term in office, Republicans lost 40 House seats. A Marist poll conducted in September that year found a similar picture of the electorate compared to now. Registered voters preferred Democratic congressional candidates by 12 points, 50% to 38%. That lead narrowed in polling over the following two months, settling at 6 points in the final pre-election survey. Of course, margins seen in September polling are a snapshot of the mood of voters, not a forecast of electoral outcomes. Unprecedented redistricting efforts have also narrowed the field of competitive House races since 2018, blunting the potential size of any wave election. "I don't think 40 seats is remotely in play," Miringoff said. A gain of a dozen House seats would be a good outcome for Democrats, he said. Democrats now lead on issues Republicans used to own Gas prices are shown in Great Neck, New York, on Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Shannon Stapleton/ Reuters For a party in power, a referendum election would be more survivable if voters still trusted it to handle the toughest issues of governing. They don't, according to this latest poll. Voters say Democrats would do a better job handling the economy, gas prices and foreign policy. On immigration, the Republican edge has evaporated. In what has become an election focused on affordability, 42% of voters say Democrats would do a better job handling the economy while 34% say Republicans. articles.title_orig: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.title_zh: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.content_orig:
A White House makeover that has long raised eyebrows is now prompting questions about fire codes. The Washington Post reports that architect James McCrery II stepped away from designing President Trump's planned East Wing ballroom last fall after warning that Trump's preferred layout didn't offer enough emergency exits, fire barriers, or bathrooms for its proposed capacity—concerns that McCrery believed put it at odds with nationally recognized safety standards, according to internal documents and people familiar with the situation.
Trump's reported response when told that codes applied, in addition to saying that codes don't apply to White House builds: "I am the code." The Post details how Trump personally annotated floor plans with a Sharpie—expanding the ballroom footprint, erasing service corridors and staircases, and favoring Versailles-style flourishes, including millions in gold leaf. Unlike typical major White House projects, this one has been funneled through the Executive Residence rather than agencies like the General Services Administration, limiting outside oversight.
The White House says safety compliance has been a priority, and that "life safety issues have been addressed," denying that McCrery's exit was over code disputes. McCrery, for his part, says in a statement that "having completed the earliest designs, I stepped aside and a new firm was engaged," adding he was "truly grateful for that honor and for the rich experience of working for [Trump]."
The current architect, Shalom Baranes Associates, isn't talking. Meanwhile, the AP reports that Trump also wants to build a drone port on top of the ballroom, including "missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops." Trump told reporters on Tuesday that the ballroom project was ahead of schedule and under budget, "despite reports of rising costs," per Newsweek.
